tion question, I will, with your permission, leave any other matters until the close of this debate, as I may have omitted particulars which I may then wish to refer to. I thank the House for the kind attention they have given me, and I close by repeating what I have already said, that if ever Canada is to become commercially great, we must take up these important improvements without any more delay.

speakeroldname: Mr. THOMAS G. RODDICK (Montreal, St. Antoine).
speechtext:
In rising, Mr. Speaker, to make a few remarks on this question of transportation, especially in its relation to the city of Montreal and the St. Lawrence river from Montreal to the sea, it is a pleasure for me to feel, as my hon. friend from the St. Lawrence division, (Mr. Bicker-dike) evidently felt that this is not a political or a party question. Any discussion in this House on the importance of our great waterway and the establishment of a national port in Canada should never be lowered to the level of party, but be considered, from start to finish, as a patriotic and national question. My hon. friend has gone so thoroughly over the ground that but little remains for me to say. We are here, Sir, to-day not to find fault with the government, not to blame those ministers who are administering the two great Departments of Marine and Fisheries and Public Works-the two departments to which we appeal for assistance on this occasion. But we are here to implore, to beg practically on our knees for something to be done which will improve the facilities for navigation of the St. Lawrence and the terminal facilities of the port of .Montreal. We want if possible to have to-day a declaration, a definite statement from the government, as to what amount of money is likely to be expended in making the city of Montreal the national port of Canada, in making it a free port, and in so improving the facilities for navigation on the St. Lawrence that confidence will be restored to the shipping and commercial Interests of this country. That confidence has been practically lost, not alone by the shipping interests of Canada, but of Great Britain and of France, and I might even say of Germany. We find that our trade is terribly handicapped by the high insurance rates charged on ships and cargoes coming into and going out of the St. Lawrence.
I have taken a little trouble to get some information on this subject, and although I may be going over the same ground as my hon. friend who preceded me, I think that the importance of this subject furnishes me with a good excuse. I have been furnished by a friend of mine, of wide commercial experience-and I may say a gentleman who lias always supported our friends on the other side-with this Information :
Marine insurance to the St. Lawrence is more than double that to American ports; for in-

stance, where the insurance is 4i per cent to, say, Baltimore, we have to pay from 9 to 10 per cent, and even 11 per cent, on the steamers employed in the St. Lawrence route, which means on a vessel costing, say, $500,000, making five voyages in the season, extra insurance of $5,000 per voyage, or $25,000 per year.
One of the large companies employed in the St. Lawrence, in fixing their risk for the ensuing year, found (to use the expression of. the owners) ' that the St. Lawrence stank in the nostrils of the underwriters.' When it was pointed out that the government was going to improve the gulf and river, the underwriters stated ' that they would wait until that time came round.'
This difference of insurance is no exaggeration, as the company referred to arranged the premiums on their Montreal, Baltimore and Newport News steamers at the same time.
Regarding tramp tonnage, we have to say that while we are able to charter all the steamers required for our trade on the Atlantic coast, we find it next to impossible to get steamers for our Montreal trade, the charterers only stating in letter received from them this week that the trouble regarding Montreal was that the owners would not face the insurance charge on the St. Lawrence route.
Seventy-five per cent of Lloyd's underwriters will not look at the St. Lawrence, either for hulls or freight.
That proves tbat we are driving away trade from this country every day, and when it can be proved, as has been already stated by my hon. friend who preceded me, that whole lines of steamers are leaving our shores every day, one can readily understand the necessity for immediate action. My hon. friend has given us the names of the steamship lines which have left Montreal, and I am very sorry to hear that others are likely to follow suit. This means that something must be done, and warrants us in demanding that the administration declare positively and definitely what they intend doing. It will not do to put us off this time with the ordinary stereotyped statement which ministers use too often, I am sorry to say, that this matter will be taken into their serious consideration. We want to get something definite, and that without delay, as to the policy likely to be adopted.
Other reasons tvhy shipping is leaving our river, besides the high rates of insurance, are the feeling of insecurity in traversing the St. Lawrence route, the wretched terminal facilities in the port of Montreal, and the high harbour duties. The terminal facilities have already been referred to at considerable length, but I might refer to a few points which have not been touched upon. In the first place, our wharfs are all of too low a level, which makes practically impossible the building of permanent sheds, such as are found in other terminals. The sheds, of course, as you are aware, are removed every spring because otherwise the ice would carry them off. High level wharfs are then of the utmost importance and should be included in any scheme sub-

mitred by tlie government or the minister in charge of this department.
We find that the transportation of cattle, which my hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdilce) so thoroughly understands, is a matter of considerable importance also. I am informed on the best authority that because of the fact that cattle have to be bustled about and must pass through narrow streets for long distances down to the wharfs, they practically lose In value from $2 to $5 per head before they leave the port of Montreal. That is a very serious question and one to which consideration should be given. Another matter which was brought to my attention the other day was that the flour which was shipped to Montreal is practically decreased in value by about $4 per car-load from the fact that there are no storage facilities and the flour must be left in the cars until shipping can take place, and then it costs about $4 a car to carry this flour to the ships. At the very highest, a charge of $2 should cover the transhipment. Then, to our lumber friends I would say that we have no facilities for piling lumber in the harbour of Montreal. The consequence is that the purchaser finds that he is obliged to pay for demurrage to the extent of $10 or $12 for the boat or barge on which the lumber is carried. This, of course, should not be. The question of grain is, of course, the most important one-I run over these items hoping that they will be dealt with at greater length by hon. gentlemen who follow me. I am convinced from my conversation with commercial friends and from the fact that the council of the Board of Trade of Montreal recommended that course, that probably the best plan is to have the government build the elevator. Many schemes have been suggested, but this is the one which the council of the board of trade, after long consideration has recommended. These elevators should be built at a suitable point, and, if possible should be approached by an elevated railway, so that the general traffic on the wharfs might not be so much disturbed. The idea in having the government build the elevators is to prevent the possibility of foreign contractors intervening and foreign capital being used for this purpose. It is not thought desirable that the scheme that has been for so long before the public, the Conners scheme, or even the Wolvin scheme, should be carried out, but it is their opinion-I give it as theirs-that the government should build the elevators. One might be built at a time, or two might be built at the same time as might be thought desirable. A charge sufficient to pay the interest and cover the working expenses should alone be made. If it is found at the end of the year that the charges are too low. they could be raised to cover these two points.; if too high, they could be lowered so as to cover barely working expenses and in-101
terest. In the event of the government refusing to ibulM- the elevators, it seems to me that the best thing would be that they should utilize money that is in their hands belonging to the city of Montreal for that purpose, as suggested by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence, or the scheme that is proposed by Mr. Crathern, of Montreal, that the harbour board should borrow $1,000,000 from the government and build the elevator. I am obliged, however, as a man without practical experience to come to the conclusion that the council of the board of trade may get credit for having thought this matter over very seriously. In all probability their scheme is the one that will give the most satisfaction. A third reason why ships are leaving our ports is that the condition of navigation is so unsatisfactory from Montreal to the sea that ship-owners will not run the risks that they would run if they adopted this route.
Mr. CIIAIiLTOX. May I ask my hon. friend in what portion of the river tlie conditions of navigation are particularly unsatisfactory-above or below Quebec ?

I am coming to that. In the first place. I believe that the channel should be 30 feet deep, as my hon. friend has stated, but I think I would add another 100 feet to the width, making it 600 feet, instead of 500 feet, as, I think, was suggested. We know that one of the great bugbears to captains and pilots is the fear that, in passing down this narrow channel, they will strike one side or the other, and if a little side wind happens to be blowing, with that and the current behind them, they are almost certain to be veered around [DOT]and jammed across the channel, and thus block navigation for hours or even days. We must remember that when the present channel was dug, the ships were very much smaller than they are now. I think we ought to legislate a little for posterity in this matter. If we are going to make any alterations in this channel, we should make it fit to take the Celtic for instance, of
20.000	tons up to the city of Montreal. And, unless you arrange upon a generous scale, you will find that in a few years, ten years or so, shippers will tell you that you have made a mistake and that the' channel should be 600 feet instead of 500 feet in width. That is the great difficulty, I think, in the navigation between Montreal and Quebec-the channel question. The lighting question, which also has been referred to so fully, deserves a word. The lighting of the river immediately below Montreal is hardly sufficient. We find that ships-they may be large freight steamers, or even passenger steamers-come up to the foot of the current, only three or four miles from' the wharfs, and they have to remain there all night, whereas if we had the river properly lighted, these steamers could come up to



the wharfs and a great deal of work could be done during the night. For shippers are obliged, owing to the cramped condition to the harbour, to work night and day. In fact, most of the work is done at night from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. Proper lighting would facilitate matters very much, and I would make that suggestion to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. These are the only points that I have to suggest on the route down as far as Quebec. My hon. friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Biekerdike) went so fully into the *Question of lighting and signals that 1 do not intend to touich upon it. He has explained fully how necessary it is that certain changes should be made. One point which I hope every hon. gentlemen heard, was that there is a general consensus of opinion that wherever there is a light there should also be a fog signal. That, I think, should be made very clear.
I know the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is aware of that fact, because he referred to it the other day when the delegation met him, and I hope he will see it carried out, that the sirens are made loud enough, and that the variety in sound is made great enough so that captains can tell, in a dense fog, and in the absence of a light, exactly where they are.
Now, there is another subject which was not referred to by my hon. friend, but which I consider of great importance. I have already referred to it from my seat in the House during the last parliament, that is, a hydrographic survey of the St. Lawrence river. A hydrographic survey of the river means that the tides and currents should be thoroughly studied, and that the depth of water should be ascertained and charted. The question of tides and currents, I know, has been ignored in some quarters. I will not say it has been ignored by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, but I know that he has not felt as keenly on that subject, and has not realized the necessity, as some others have done. Some of his predecessors felt as he did, that it was not a matter of great importance, and others have felt so. I hope he will be induced to study the question, and that ho will realize the great necessity of a hydrographic survey of the lower St. Lawrence.
I find, in looking over this book which has been presented to members of this House, known as the Shipping Inquiry, and which has been so fully referred to by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence, that twenty out of thirty-two captains, I think, whose evidence was taken and is reported, had something to say in regard to a hydrographic survey of the St. Lawrence. When you get | twenty out of over thirty-two sea captains going out of their way to say that the hydrographic survey of the St. Lawrence needs some attention, I think there is proof that the matter is an important one in their view. Some of the evidence is very specific.

For instance, Capt. Brodie, of the Sarma-tian of the Allan line, suggested that a good survey be made in the gulf, and that soundings should be taken between Greenway Island and Cape Ray. Capt. Farewell, who has been in the service for ten years, is of opinion that the gulf should be entirely resurveyed, as the soundings made by him did not correspond with those found on the chart. That is a very serious matter. Capt. Baxter believes that the lower St. Lawrence ought to be surveyed more and a fresh chart provided. He finds that the soundings on tiie chart differ altogether from what he got himself on the southern route. Capt. Ferris considers a hydrographic survey of the gulf advisable. He finds some things on the charts inside the gulf not always as found in actual work on me ship ; nor has he found the currents setting, as a rule, as shown on the charts. Capt. Taylor considers that the charts should be extended fifty or sixty miles further north to provide for cases where a vessel coming from the north strikes the north of Belle Isle, in which case the master is off the chart. Evidence is given of a similar character by Captains Cole, Vipond, Dingle, Lander, Iloilo, Evans, Chapman, Minister, Wallace and Fraser, who favour a hydrographic survey of the entire gulf or of parts of the gulf. I repeat that this matter is of sufficient importance, at any rate, to justify all that has been done in this direction, and to require that we should not retrace our steps, nor, at any rate, do less than has been done. There was a vote given by this House seven or eight years ago of $15,000 for this specific purpose. That grant followed a recommendation from the British Association meeting in the city of Montreal. The association felt strongly that this matter was being neglected by the Dominion government, and after considerable delay a sum of $15,000 was voted to provide a steamer for Mr. Bell Dawson and his staff, and they have done a lot of excellent work. I find in this report for 1900, published by him, that he has had to 'depend in great measure on the fishermen for his information, because he has been unable to cover the ground, not being supplied with a steamer. Referring to the tidal currents as a whole, he says :
The strongest of the tidal currents are found on the lower St. Lawrence, where in places they attain a speed of five or six knots per hour. Also, the tidal current in the Gut of Canso runs at four knots; and in the narrowest part of Northumberland Straits, oil Cape Jourmain, at three knots per hour. The currents in these localities have not been examined by this survey, however.
A current running at the rate of six knots per hour is practically unknown to the Marine Department in this country. That, I think, is a pity, and I hope the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will see that something is done to correct that. If time per-

mitted, I could make several other references from this book to prove that some action should be taken of a decisive character, and I hope the minister will give Mr. Bell Dawson a small yacht for the purpose. He does not need a steamer, he only needs a vessel of about SO tons, and he should have plenty of time and opportunity to correct these defects in the hydrographic survey. I remember myself, as a Newfoundlander, when I used to yacht round the coast of Newfoundland as a lad, how serious these currents are. I know we used to allow our boats to drift in certain currents which we happened to be acquainted with along the southern coast ; we would put out out" fishing tackle and lie down and go to sleep without bothering ourselves as to the course of our boat, and in the morning find that we had travelled several miles. One can understand, therefore, that a want of knowledge of the tides and currents in the lower St. Lawrence has undoubtedly led to shipwrecks.
The Mariposa is generally considered to have been wrecked on account of want of knowledge of the currents, and another steamer, the Algerian, if I mistake not, was also supposed to have been wrecked for the same reason. It is the general impression of scientific men that when no explanation can be given for the drifting of a ship on the rocks, the currents are to blame. Therefore, I think this matter is of sufficient importance to induce my hon. friend to increase his vote this year in order to cover that very important ground. Now, Sir, to (sum up, because I feel that I have taken up the attention of the House too long, our intention in bringing about this discussion has been to induce the government to make Montreal a free port. One of the things that stands in the wTay of the port of Montreal is the fact that the dues are high, whereas, we know that several of the American ports, such as Portland, Boston, I think Newport News and probably Baltimore, are free to shippers. I hope the government *will take the harbour over and make it and call it the national port of Canada, and that they will also make it a free port. I maintain that Montreal should be the national port of Canada, not because I live there, but for two reasons. In the first place, it is at the head of ocean navigation. That cannot be denied. It is 180 miles nearer to the great grain centres and to the centres from which we get the most of our commerce than is the port of Quebec. I have no quarrel with Quebec. On the contrary, nothing would give me greater pleasure than to see Quebec flourish as Montreal will flourish, and there is no reason why Quebec should not share this prosperity with Montreal. I believe that when the great scheme outlined by the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike), the construction of the Georgian Bay canal is carried out, not only Montreal, but Quebec, 1011
Toronto, Kingston and other cities will have good times. Whether it is desirable to speak of that now or not, I do not know. Doubtless there are others who are better able to discuss it than I am who will take it up later on. Then, Sir, I would suggest that the government should build elevators and allow the harbour board to run them and take entire charge of them. The St. Lawrence channel should be deepened to thirty feet and widened to COO feet, and the lighting of the river in the neighbourhood of Montreal should be very much improved. I may say before sitting down that a great deal of work has been done and a great deal of interest in this work has been displayed by both the hon. ministers who have to do with it. I know that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) has especially been anxious and desirous to make the city of Montreal the national port, and I think he should feel that he has this House and the country behind him. This desire is not confined to Montreal. One of the ablest speeches delivered on this subject a few weeks ago was by an hon. gentleman who lives a great distance from Montreal, who lives in the heart of an agricultural country. I speak of the hon. Deputy Speaker (Mr. Macdonald). One of the ablest speeches I listened to in this House was delivered by the hon. member for Huron. It shows that men who live at a distance from Montreal may feel that their pockets are not to be injured or their pride disturbed by supporting this great national project. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the kind hearing which you have given me.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much pleasure indeed to the addresses of the two hon. gentlemen who have preceded me. While not agreeing fully with them, I certainly agree with them to a very considerable extent, and later on, during the Course of the remarks that I have to address to this House,
I will state wherein I agree and wherein I differ. I had listened previously in this House to several discussions upon this important question, but have, myself, taken no part, in these discussions. At the same time, I have had strong convictions on the question which is now engaging the attention of the House, and I have entertained these convictions for a number of years. Now', the question is not a question "as to whether Montreal, or Quebec, or St. John, or Halifax, shall become the national port of Canada. That is not the question at all. There is a great contest going on on this continent, a very great contest indeed, in this matter of transportation, and this is perhaps one of the greatest questions that could engage the attention of the parliament of Canada. The contest is not one between rival sections of Canada or the rival ports of Canada, but the contest is one between ourselves and our great neighbours to the

south of us. The great question for Canadians is this : By what means will the produce of our farms, of our forests, of our mines and fisheries, or that portion which we export, be sent most cheaply to the countries which purchase them from us. That is the great question. The contest .will be a keen one. There is no doubt about that. To-day and for years past it has been the case that the produce of the western states has almost entirely found its way to the seaboard through American channels, and it is unfortunate that a large portion of the produce of western Canada, of Manitoba and the Xorth-west Territories, has also found its shipment through ports of the United States. Well, if the produce of Canadians to-day finds, and will ultimately find, the cheapest means of transportation to foreign markets through that channel, I have no fault to find, but we have in Canada the natural outlet not only for the products of the western portion of our own country, but for the products of the western states as well.	It devolves upon Canada to say
whether that shall be the outlet for the western country or whether it shall continually be the case that the greater portion of that shipment shall go through American channels. Now, coming immediately to make some reference to the speeches of the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me, I will say at once, in discussing the question as it affects Montreal, or Quebec, or the other ports of Canada, that I have no choice whatever.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) made the statement that up to the present time the government of Canada had expended no money on the port of Montreal. He is perhaps correct as regards the harbour of Montreal, but he cannot deny that the government of Canada have spent a very large sum of money in deepening the St. Lawrence river between the city of Montreal and Quebec. And in so far as the expenditure generally is concerned in the city of Montreal, I doubt very much indeed if that great city has not had its share of the expenditure of public money in this country. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) also said that the St. Lawrence route was the cheapest of the various routes by which the produce of the great west could reach the seaboard, but later on he referred to the Georgian Bay canal as being the best transportation system of all. Well, if I understand correctly, the Georgian Bay canal is certainly not the St. Lawrence route; it is another route eu-tirelv; it will be the Ottawa route. It appears to me, Sir, that the great question today is not so much the carriage of grain to the city of Montreal itself, ns it is the affording of facilities to handle the grain and ship it to the old country when it gets to Montreal. I have been informed by the railway companies and the other carriers who take grain from the west to our seaports, that they can to-day bring a much Mr. EDWARDS.
larger quantity of grain and other produce to the head of navigation than there are ships to take them from Canadian ports. That question I will deal with more fully a little later on. In a great measure I agree with the statements of the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me, as to the necessity of improving the St. Lawrence route in order to accommodate a larger number of ocean-going steamers. There is no question whatever that in so far as shipments from our lower ports are concerned, the St. Lawrence route ' has been somewhat of a barrier, because the insurance rates on the St. Lawrence route have discriminated very materially against all our Canadian trade. Suggestions have been made for the improvement of the existing insurance conditions by means of initiating new methods of insurance, but I may say at once that I do not agree with any proposition of that kind.
Hear hear.

cept that I think the city of Quebec is the natural ocean port for the St. Lawrence river. The city of Montreal is not to-day the natural port, nor will it ever be. The cheapest means by which we can transport our products to foreign markets is by the great ships that are now being built, and the still larger ships that will be built in the future. I believe that when proper provision is made, these great ships can come with all speed and safety to the port of Quebec; but you can deepen the St. Lawrence river as deep as you please between Montreal and Quebec, and it will never be a safe route for these very large vessels. My hon. friend (Mr. Roddick) un-. wittingly gave the reasons therefor, when he said that those large ships require a great deal more sea room than other ships, and, Sir, that sea room they never can possibly have in the artificial channel between Montreal and Quebec. For these reasons I state again: that I believe that all the money that has been expended in deepening the channel between Montreal and Quebec is wasted money, and that any further money expended in that direction will be wasted also.
There is another defect, so far as the development of shipments from Canada is concerned and it is a very great defect. I know perfectly well that many hon. gentlemen will not agree with me when I make the statement I am about to make ; but that does not hinder me from making the statement. One of the great reasons why we have not a greater number of vessels coming to Quebec, Montreal and the other ports of Canada is because of the tariff arrangements that have existed in Canada for many years. If Canada is to export its products in the cheapest possible way, there must be cargoes for the vessels both ways. The great reason why there are not more vessels coming to the ports of the St. Lawrence is that they cannot bring inward cargoes ; and therefore a surplus of our grain and other products has to-day to go to other ports to secure shipment.
Then, why is it that the port of New York, in a strong protectionist country, has an immense traffic ?

The hon. gentlemau thinks he has given me a very difficult question to answer ; but it is not at all difficult. To answer it I have to deal more largely with a certain question than I expected. If there is a country in the world so constituted as to withstand the iniquities of protection, it is the United States. If there is one country in the world geographically situated so as not to stand the iniquities of protection, it is Canada.
WTe are exactly alike.

The hon. gentleman perhaps does not know that notwithstanding
its tariff restrictions, the United States buys more per head from foreign countries than Canada does ; and consequently there are more cargoes brought to that country in proportion to the shipping from it than there are to Canada as against the shipping from Canada. Now, my hon. friend from the St. Lawrence division of Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) stated that he would give a still greater preference to British goods ; but how did he say he would give that preference ? He said he would give it to goods only that came to Canada through the ports of Canada.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman says hear, hear. This is a free country, and every gentleman has a perfect right to entertain any views he pleases ; but, Mr. Speaker, that is not my view upon trade. My view upon trade is simply this : Give us the greatest possible freedom of trade, and then there will be no question of preferences of any kind.
Why do you not give it ? You are in power.

Mr. Speaker, the party to which the hon. gentleman is attached is responsible for imposing on Canada the greatest disease that was ever imposed on any country. I am a free trader of free traders, a radical free trader ; but I have never on any occasion said that I would apply the antidote in such a way as to kill the patient. Under the iniquitous system created by hon. gentlemen opposite Canada has suffered for many years. It will take years to wipe out the iniquity ; but, Mr. Speaker, the iniquity will be wiped out
I rise to a point of order. I want to know if the hon. gentleman is entitled to charge the opposition with iniquity.
I understood the hon. member's remark to apply to the system or the policy, not to any individual member.

It will take years, Mr. Speaker ; and, free trader as I am, I stated years ago, when hon. gentlemen opposite occupied seats on this side of the House, that it would be impossible in a day or in a year to wipe out that great iniquity.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said he would do it.

I have nothing to do with what the Minister of Trade and Commerce may have said. This is a question on which I have always been able to think for myself, and I have done so independently of the views or contentions of any one ; and I think it would be a grand thing for

Canada, if not only the people of Canada, but the members of this House would study this question to the extent that I have studied it. There are those who believe that if we had larger imports from other countries, our manufactures in this country would decrease. Not at all. Let us give to Canada every facility, by cheap transportation, by allowing the farmer who is the great producer of the wealth of this country to buy what he wants as freely as he sells his products, and the development of this country will be so great that it will be but a few years when we shall manufacture ten times what we manufacture today. If this country is to prosper and develop, the men who are producing its wealth must not be hampered as they have been hampered in the past, and are still hampered in a very much less degree. 1 may be asked, are you satisfied with the distance the Liberal party have gone in the direction of removing this iniquity ? I say yes. They have gone in that respect as far as they could go under existing circumstances. 1 find no fault-none whatever. But, I say this, that protection still exists in this country in a limited degree, and I as a free trader will never be satisfied till the last vestige of that iniquity, imposed on this country by hon. gentlemen opposite, is removed. What is the use of improving our facilities for transport ? What is the use of developing our railways and our canals, if you hamper trade and do not allow those canals and railways to carry traffic inwards as well as outwards ? Why, it is perfectly ridiculous. There is no use whatever in improving the St. Lawrence route, if the conditions are such as to prevent vessels coming from England and other countries with imports which can carry away our produce in return. I refer to this point because it is incidental to the subject under discussion, and I repeat that there is no use whatever in our going on improving our waterways unless we have such freedom of trade as will enable those waterways to be used.
There is another question to which reference has been made, and that is, the Georgian Bay canal. I was a little surprised to find that my hon. friend from the St. Lawrence division of Montreal (Mr. Roddick! was so large in his views. He said that the further we could go into the interior with our ships, the better for the country. But, what of Montreal in that case ? There is, perhaps, no one thing that can be done in this country that would have such a revolutionary effect upon the conditions of Canada as the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. I believe that its construction to a depth of 20 feet would make it the greatest developer of Canada.
Can It be done ?

I do not know. But, if the engineering and financial conditions per-Mr. EDWARDS.
mit of its being done, I believe that a 20-foot canal, constructed from Georgian Bay to Montreal, will be the greatest thing for Canada that could possibly be done. But, would that result in vessels loading at Georgian Bay and going across the ocean ? I think it would be, but only to a limited extent. I believe that the great carriers on the lakes would go to Montreal and Quebec, and other ports on the eastern coast, and there discharge into larger vessels. And I am further of the opinion, that such a scheme would result in an inflow of a large portion of American goods for the western states over this route, and if that should happen, the inward cargoes would be supplied. Would this detract from the importance of Montreal ? Not at all. In order that our cities throughout Canada may be developed, we require to build up our country, and I do not think there is any other means by which this country could be developed to so great an extent as by the building of this canal. To say that Montreal is going to go backwards is absurd. My candid opinion is, that Montreal will always bear the same relative position to Canada as New York does to the United States. It is bound to continue the great commercial centre of Canada, and Quebec will be the second city, with Ottawa third and Winnipeg fourth.
Where is Toronto V
Toronto is not in it. 1 have nothing against the great city of Toronto, which is the capital of the province in which I live.
What about Halifax ?

Well, it will come in some way, but the Georgian Bay canal, I believe, will be built ; and when it is. the result will be, in my opinion, what I have stated. I have no preference for any one city in Canada, except that if I wanted to choose a city in which to live, I would like to live in the city of Quebec. Next to that, I would like to live in Halifax.
Next, Toronto.

I would like, before living in the city of Toronto, to have its views enlarged and its bigotry lessened. I think I have said all that I desire to say now on this question. I am anxious to see Canada developed in every possible way. I want to see the St. Lawrence route improved in every possible way, but I do not want to see an artificial channel built from Quebec to Montreal, because I believe it was never required, and is not required to-day.

I would like, Mr. Speaker, to ask the last speaker (Mr. Edwards) how it is that the city of Quebec, although it has received from the Dominion government some

$5,000,000 or $8,000,000, cannot, even with the expenditure of all this money, be made a national port ? I fail to understand the objection of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) to the improvement of the channel between Montreal and Quebec. It seems to me that the deepening of that channel is as much in the interests of the people of the west, as it is in the interests of the people of Montreal themselves. Looking over the record, I find that in the past fifteen or twenty years, the government has expended on canals and harbours throughout (this Dominion some $20,000,000, of which Montreal has never received one cent. It seems to me. therefore, high time that Montreal should take a decided stand, and insist on getting what it is entitled to. Compare the customs revenues received at that port with those received at other ports in the Dominion. In the year 1900, the revenue from customs duties alone received at Montreal, amounted to $9,000,000, whereas the customs dues received at the port of Quebec only amounted to $961,000, at Halifax, $1,252,000. and at St. John. $S97,000, or, in other words, the revenue collected in Montreal was three times as large as that of the other three ports I have mentioned.
I have no desire to detain the House by entering into a long discussion of the subject before us, after the very thorough treatment it has received at the hands of the two representatives from the city of Montreal who preceded me. It is clear that what the board of trade to-day is most interested in, is the erection of elevators, and I feel confident that this government will see the justice of their demands, and meet the views of all those who are interested in the supremacy of our great national port. I regret that one discordant note with regard to the improving of the channel between Montreal and Quebec should have been sounded by the hon. gentleman who last addressed the House (Mr. Edwards), but I have no doubt that the views in that respect to which he gave expression are not those of the great majority of hon. members, and that this House and the government will appreciate the necessity, in the interests of the whole country, of doing everything possible to improve our great national highway.

I thought we had pretty well threshed out this question when the subject of transpor-: tation was up before the House some time ago, but I must crave the indulgence of the House if I rise to reply to some remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Gallery) and of the hon. member for the St. Lawrence division of Montreal (Mr. Roddick). The hon. gentleman who last spoke said that the government had not done anything for the port of Montreal. I was carried back a period of nearly thirty years, when the same 'question was debated
pretty warmly, not in this House, but in the Dominion Board of Trade. Among those who were present at that meeting were Hon. John Young, Hon. Thomas White, Hugh McLennan, and Mr. Cramp. I do not think that at that time you could find four abler or better representatives of the city of Montreal. These gentlemen took part in a discussion with the members from Quebec and Kingston. A resolution was moved on behalf of Quebec, which I would like to read, for it is very short, and because I happened to be there and to move this resolution. I considered at that time that it was quite worthy of consideration, and I believe that it is as worthy of consideration by this House to-day before we continue the very extravagant and costly work of deepening and widening Lake St. Peter. The resolution reads as follows :
That this board would urge the government to lose no time in carrying out the improving of the highway from the west to the ocean ; and that it is also desirable, before it is committed to any scheme for deepening Lake St. Peter, to consider whether the harbour of Quebec could not be utilized and made capable, at a comparatively small outlay, to accommodate and tranship the commodities from Europe to our western towns, and also the grain and produce of our western towns, to Europe, and also the grain and produce of the west to Europe, at a less cost and with greater economy ihan by an extensive and costly work, such as deepening Lake St. Peter.
A statement was made at that time which I think this House might well consider today. Wheat can be carried from the west to Quebec for 1 cent per bushel more than to Montreal and from Quebec to Europe for 3 cents per bushel less than from Montreal to Europe. Thus there is a saving on shipments by Quebec of 2 cents per bushel. Now, Mr. McLennan is reported as having made this very emphatic statement. He
-begged leave to correct the gentlemen from Quebec and Hamilton; he (Mr. McLennan) had already stated on this floor that Montreal did not now desire to have any public money spent for the purpose of deepening Lake St. Peter.
He was followed by Hon. John Young in a similar strain and also by Hon. Thomas White, of whom it is reported :
He discountenanced the idea of asking the government to deepen the channel through Lake St. Peter, and said if the government would grant them the power, the people of Montreal would do It themselves.
In what year was that ?

It was in 1873. Mr. White also said :
Let the Quebec people afford the facilities for doing western trade and they would get It ; and if they outstripped Montreal in the competition they would deserve their reward ; but they ought not to come to this board and ask support for a movement that was the same in principle, as that they had denounced when

asked by others. Why should they ask the government to survey the harbour of Quebec unless they were to Improve It? Why not let Quebec survey her own harbour, just as Montreal did?
I do not admit that it would be better for each harbour to improve its own advantages. But again I claim that when the hon. members from Montreal stand up and declare in this House that the government have done nothing for Montreal-not one dollar-I think that what my hon. friend from the St. Lawrence stated
Does the hon. gentleman contradict that statement ?

Most distinctly. I point out what the Montreal delegates of that time claimed. They distinctly discon-tenanced the idea of asking the government to spend one penny in deepening Lake St. Peter. I am not going to say that I follow these gentlemen to that extreme. I have said over and over again that it is the duty of this country to widen and deepen such channels and to give every facility for bringing the largest steamers up from the ocean to Montreal if necessary, but, if it can be done at a much less cost to the whole Dominion, then I claim they should not carry it beyond the harbour of Quebec. But, if it cannot be done cheaper, if it will not be a greater advantage to the large steam barges and their consorts to come from the far west to Quebec and for the oceangoing steamers to load in Quebec than to go to Montreal-which I claim is the common sense view to take of it-we will join cordially with Montreal in having the channel deepened and widened, for we must offer to the far west every possible advantage for bringing the trade by the St. Lawrence.
In what condition is the harbour of Quebec to-day ? What would it require to do this trade ?
It is a credit to Quebec.
Is it ready now to do this trade ? Are there the facilities ?
Everything.
Elevators and everything else ?
There are two.
Yes, but one is
No good.

No, it is a very fine elevator, but it is not situated advantageously for the winter work and we should have one differently situated ; I would build another elevator. Then, with steamers coming to Quebec, they could come to these elevators and get loaded.
One or two more points and I have done. Let me repeat that the real evil, the great reason why the St. Lawrence route is losing trade is because of the high rates of insurance on trade by this route. I say that if ever a government was warranted in taking extraordinary measures to remove a difficulty, this government should do its utmost to do away with this discrimination by the underwriters against our trade. I believe there is no more danger in going up the St. Lawrence than in going to Boston or New York. We should make all reasonable improvements. We should have the lighting of the St. Lawrence route so perfect that no creature could say that a new light is needed here or an additional signal there. We should have it as nearly perfect as possible from Belle Isle to Quebec. I am satisfied that the loss of the Scotsman would never have taken place if we had had a light on the north-east corner of Belle Isle.
Why should the hon. gentleman say that when it is contradicted by the evidence ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Because I know the advantages that a light so placed would afford.
The Scotsman was lost on account of the fog.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But a light would penetrate a fog for some distance.
How far ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I should say half a mile. However, I do not wish to get into a dispute with my colleague on these matters. But I do say that in approaching Belle Isle in a northern course you cannot see the lights there at all. I have observed it myself over and over again, and seen the danger that exists in coming on the northern passage. I do not want to make light of the improvements that have taken place. But the House must recollect that the old appliances, particularly the lighthouses, were not made for steamers going at 10 or 15 knots an hour, they were only made for sailing ships. They are a remnant of the old days. Now it is necessary at present to expend a large sum of money in fitting up strong lights, and sirens also, because wherever there is a light there should be a siren, so that if there is a fog the seamen may hear it, and if the weather is clear they may see the light. Provided with these, I be-

lieve our river will be no more dangerous for vessels coming up than for vessels going to Boston or Portland. Any one who is acquainted with the approaches to New York knows there is considerable danger of running on the flats, and steamers have run on shore going to New York. I do not mean to say that we shall ever make the St. Lawrence or any other place absolutely free from risk and danger, as risk is a natural accompaniment of danger. But I do maintain that the St. Lawrence can be made safe for navigation both in summer and winter. If we can only get steamers to come to Quebec in winter, the effect will be that instead of insurance companies raising their rates on the 1st of September, if the rates are raised at all, it will not be until November or December. September and October will naturally be looked upon as summer rates, because you can navigate the St. Lawrence up to December. I am putting that in a guarded way, supposing that the months of February and March will not be safe for ordinary steamers, and we can never have winter navigation unless it is by ordinary first-class steamers. Anything special will be a failure, you can never work winter navigation unless with our ordinary first-class tramp steamers, steamers that will class A 1 for 20 years, just ordinary heavy strongly-built steamers.
I do not understand the minister clearly. How does he intend to work this winter navigation, with special appliances or with the vessels themselves ?

With the vessels themselves, anything special will kill it. 1 have no faith that we can have winter navigation if anything special is required. I will make a suggestion to my colleagues when the time comes that all we should, provide for is the payment of any extra insurance for four or five steamers that may come out and load entirely at Quebec and go back. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company tell us that if we can only secure winter navigation they will send 380,000 tons of produce out by the St. Lawrence between December and May.
Does the hon. minister say that we can compete with Portland and New York in winter ?

Certainly, I believe we cap. But 1 will say that we must proceed cautiously, we must make some provision beforehand. The hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike), spoke of that permanent pier at the Traverse. That permanent pier renders it possible now to bring up steamers, but it was not possible before. Only three years ago a steamer came up and, not finding lightships there-because they had to be removed on account of ice-she went round to Halifax and was there discharged. This
spring three steamers came up the river before the light ships were in place, and had it not been for the permanent pier that was put there last year by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, they could not have come up, they would have had to go back. Without that permanent pier in the Traverse, I would not for a moment think of bringing up this question and dwelling upon it as I have done, both to-night and on a previous occasion.
I would like to say one word to our friends from Montreal. We in Quebec have no desire whatever to lessen their prosperity. My contention is that there is more trade than can foe accommodated at Montreal, Three Rivers, Sorel, or any other port in the river. We get a small share, we have never done more than 7 per cent of the western trade. We are willing to admit that Montreal may be a national port, but we call Quebec an international port. These two ports not only should take all the trade of this country, but they can draw the trade of the great grain-growing states of the west, such as Minnesota and Illinois, and get a share of their produce. Quebec for years was satisfied with its timber trade, but the forests are becoming depleted of their timber, and now we have got to look for something else; we are going to look for grain, and I believe that we shall carry it.
What about the railway rates, are they satisfactory to you ?
I think we have nothing to complain of in any way, and we are going forward, we shall take our proper place as a distributing port.

What about double tracking the Intercolonial Railway and making Halifax a national port ? That is what ought to be done. The solution of the problem is not in Quebec or in Montreal, but it is in double-tracking the Intercolonial Railway, reducing the rates, and taking the trade to Halifax.

Well, I shall not say anything against helping Halifax, and Sydney, and perhaps one or two other ports in Nova Scotia, because the whole country will benefit from it. But, as I said before, the only fault I can find with my colleagues is that they have not spent enough in that direction, they should have spent more money instead of less.
Now, I would like to say one word about the iee-!brifl,ge. The hon. member for St. Lawrence division stated that he hoped the government would take means to break the ice-bridge and not allow it to take at Cap Rouge. I am quite certain that when the piers of the bridge at Quebec are planted, there will be an ice-bridge formed very early in the season; but that ice-bridge, instead of being an impediment or a drawback, will on the contrary enable us to have

navigation up to Montreal earlier in the spring than we did before, and why ? If you do not get an ordinary ice-bridge you get later what we call a jam-bridge. That bridge which is formed at Cap Rouge to-day is formed of the ice coming down the river all the way from Three Rivers, when large battures, at high t de are carried down the river and it goes up again with the next tide, and it follows this course all winter going up and down the river until a very low tide with strong easterly winds causes these masses of ice to jam at Cap Rouge and piles up 80 feet thick. I think I said 60 feet the last time I spoke, but I did so because some one said 60 feet and some one said 40. It was something like the story of the foxes' tails. Well, as it is so near six o'clock. I will keep the story of the foxes' tails for another occasion.
I will only say this and I have done, that when the natural bridge forms the ice is never more than four or five feet thick and that bridge across the river prevents drifting ice in great masses going down into the harbour and being sent floating up and down. After the bridge has formed early in the season our harbour is free of ice ia winter. The channel is quite free. Tim batture ice forms along the wharfs and coves and it is a great safeguard ; other wise, the ice moving down from up the river in the stream with such force that it woliM carry away every wharf in the harbour, but the batture ice forms a sort of guide-way for it. The ice on both sides of the stream is polished quite smooth for miles from Cap Rouge to where it leaves Quebec and makes for the Island of Orleans, but a jam bridge remains much longer and resists all effort to mine it. I would like to have said more but it being six o'clock I will reserve the balance for another occasion.

On section 6,

I gave expression to my views on this clause in the committee, and I desire to repeat them now to this House. I do not think it is the business of a railway company to go into the acquisition of mines and timber limits and things of that sort, and my intention is to test the opinion of the House on this clause. This is a railway which at the present time extends sixty miles up the Gatineau river, and it is suggested to continue it to James Bay. I believe, in fact, that a charter has already been given for that purpose, This railway company has made two or three attempts already, in amendments to their railway charter, to get provision to enable them to become possessors of water powers, of timber limits, and of mines, that they might deal therein. In so far as a railway company may acquire timber or mines for the construction of their railway, I find no fault with that whatever. Railway companies must necessarily get from parliament great powers of expropriation, and being as they are common carriers, I claim that they have no right whatever to engage in commerce and manufacture and compete with concerns already established in such industries. That is the principle of the opposition which I offered to the present Bill. In giving a railway power to manufacture timber for the purpose of the construction of their railway, that does not all necessitate the railway company dealing in timber limits, but I can see no reason why, so far as the construction of a railway is concerned, the company should have power to deal in mines.

I ask the committee to consider this question as to whether it is right and proper that this company should have the powers that it is proposed to give them under this Bill.
Is there not a limitation to the company doing this for the purpose of its railway and its business ?

I do uot consider that the limitation covers the ground at all. The provision is that for the purposes of the railway and its business, the company may acquire timber limits and mines and buy and sell these properties and may deal in them. It may think that for the purposes of its business it should go into manufacturing, and then if any one wished to pursue the matter, they would have to bring the case into the courts to determine whether they had such power _or not.
I would like to hear the chairman of the Railway Committee on that point.

The hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is quite right. All the powers referred to by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) which were applied for originally in the charter, have been removed, and the powers under clause 0 are limited in connection with the railway and the purposes of its business. My hon. friend (Mr. Edwards seems to think that the expression ' business of the company,' would enable it to go into lumbering, other than for the purpose of the undertaking which would be to get material for the construction of the road. Personally, I do not think there is anything in that contention. There would be no objection to use the word ' undertaking ' instead of ' business ' if any hon. member thinks it material that the change should be made. As the Bill has been amended there is not the slightest doubt, from the experience we have had, that the powers granted under clause 6 are limited to the purposes of the railway company. Further than that, in this particular Bill, as it was contended that the company might have for the purposes named in this clause, the powers of expropriation under the Railway Act, the Bill was amended so as to make it clear, that the powers of expropriation would not apply under clause 6. There is that further special protection incorporated in this Bill.

Might I ask that the clause be again read to the House V
The CHAIRMAN (Mr. Flint) read the clause.

The intention of the promoters of this Bill is to get from the government certain timber limits as a bonus for the construction of this road, and the wording of that clause is devised exactly
for the purpose of allowing them to go into the manufacture of lumber and pulp or anything they may require to do. It is very cunningly devised. I see through the whole scheme. I understand it well.
That has been struck out.	.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, it has not. The acquisition of timber limits is not struck out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, that is not struck out.
I think we could easily put in something that would satisfy the member for Russell.
We are not here to satisfy ; we are here to legislate.

I think the hon. member for Russell is unduly cautious in a matter of this kind. The distinction he draws between railway corporations and trading corporations is one which, of course, ought to be maintained in granting companies charters ; but, when the privileges asked by this company are limited, as they are to some extent, by the use of the words ' for the use of the company and in connection with its business,' it seems to me that the rights of individuals who may be engaged in business of that kind are sufficiently guarded. But that is not all. The right of expropriation ha-s been thought necessary to be given to railway companies, so long as they make ample compensation so as not to do injustice to any parties ; but, that right is not granted to this company in connection with these particular matters. As it has no right to expropriate, but only a right to hold property when it gets it by purchase, I fail to see the objection which the hon. member for Russell so strenuously presses on the House. Moreover, I think we have in other instances granted powers just as ample as those proposed to be granted to this company. Therefore, I hope the hon. member for Russell will withdraw his objection.

I think there is, perhaps, something in the point which the hon. gentleman takes, which deserves a little consideration, and it is this. I do not think the object obtained by my hon. friend the chairman of the Railway Committee has been so thoroughly carried out as to remove doubts that the Expropriation Act does not apply. I do not think it is good drafting to use the word ' business ' in one place and the word ' undertaking ' in other places in the Bill. I would also suggest that instead of saying that ' nothing in this section shall be held to confer powers of expropriation under the Railway Act.' the section read : ' nothing in this Act contained shall be held to confer on the company any powers of

expropriation for any purposes or objects contained in this section.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I do not tliink the Expropriation Act applies at all to this section, even without these words. The intention of the committee was perfectly clear that the clause in the Railway Act giving power of expropriation should not apply to the powers granted in this section. So, I think the wording in the Bill, as it is before the committee, or the wording suggested by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, will be perfectly satisfactory.

House in committee on Bill (No. 58) to incorporate the Kootenay and Arrow Head Railway Company.-Mr. Galliher.
On section 13 :

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: This clause was ordered to be drafted by the clerk of the committee, and it is the usual clause granted in railway charters with regard to all the powers mentioned, except the power of owning and operating smelters and reduction works. After discussion, tiie majority of the committee seemed to think that in that country it is not objectionable that a railway should have this power. Otherwise the clause is the usual one adopted for a number of years in railway charters.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not think that railway corporations should be allowed to operate smelters. They should be confined to their work as common carriers. It appears to me that being common carriers they should lie confined to that business. If you give them power to carry on smelters in British Columbia, you will find it difficult to get outside capitalists to put money into the smelting business. I think the clause should be struck out.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Those who understand the conditions that prevail in that country know that it is one of the most difficult things to get men to take up the smelting business. The Canadian Pacific Railway have been a benefit to that country because they have gone into the smelting business. When they took possession of the Trail smelter, they reduced the prices, greatly to the advantage of the mine-owners. If they go into it again, it will be to the advantage of the country.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I fear that we are falling into the habit of endowing railway com-Sir LOUIS DAVIES.
panies that we charter with almost unlimited power, and thus laying the foundation for trouble in the future. As my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) says, a railroad is a common carrier, and it is in the public interest, in my opinion, to confine railroads as nearly as possible to their legitimate business. If railroads are to acquire timber limits, manufacture lumber, engage in mining and run smelters, the tendency and probably the result will be that the railroads will use the powers that are given them as common carriers to favour their own enterprises. It may be that under special circumstances a railroad may erect a smelter and the business may thus be started earlier than it otherwise would be. But there will hardly be any other introduction of capital for that purpose within the radius of that railroad's operation. The effect will be to deter capitalists from embarking in the same business, and in the end will thus be disastrous to the mining interests of the country in which the railroad operates.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the power of expropriation apply to the mines or anything of that kind ?

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not think so. I have no doubt that they must acquire mines just as individuals do.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The last Bill of this kind that I remember had a special clause added, that the expropriation powers should not apply to anything but the railroad. I have not heard of any such exception in this Bill.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: There are no mines mentioned in the Act as amended.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That does not matter. You incorporate a company here, and the important thing is to know whether the expropriation powers apply to the other undertakings besides the railway.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
There was a short discussion of this clause in the committee. I adhere to the view that I then took. The contention in support of the measure was the same as that brought forward by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Maxwell), that this was desirable, as it would encourage smelting, and that it would not be done if the railways were not allowed to do it. That is not satisfactory, to my mind. If the railway people desire to participate in smelting, they can form commercial companies for the purpose. I would not like to hamper any railway company in this connection, but I believe that as common carriers it is not desirable that they should carry ores from their own smelters in competition with smelters belonging to other companies. I would support the view taken by the hon. gentleman from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) and the hon. gentleman from

North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), and would urge that this clause he dropped.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I understand that they have no power under the Bill to go into mining.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Then, 1 have misunderstood the effect of the Bill.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: There is no doubt that this company has no expropriation powers except as regards their railway. The case mentioned by the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) was one in which the company applying have had many amendments to their charter during a series of years, and when their solicitor was asked whether their expropriation powers would apply to their other enterprises, he would not commit himself. Therefore, the committee Insisted on putting in a special clause to make sure. The company now under discussion did not ask for expropriation powers relating to a smelter, and we did not give them.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I would not like to give an opinion one way or another from a mere hasty glancing at the Bill. But, the railway is incorporated with power to build the railway between certain points, and as part of the undertaking certain other powers are added. If they have general powers of expropriation, and these undertakings are not excepted, would not the expropriation power apply to these undertakings ? I give no opinion myself.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies).

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No ; if the hon. gentleman will look at the Railway Act he will see that the expropriation powers are restricted to certain named things, such as acquiring right of way, acquiring station grounds, and so on.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is much better acquainted with the Railway Act than I am, and I would not give my opinion as against his. But, this new company gets powers, and a part of its undertaking is to purchase smelters and other properties If these become part of the undertaking, would not the expropriation apply ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No, as I say the powers of expropriation are strictly limited. Under the old Railway Act they could not even expropriate a gravel pit, but this was extended, because it was thought necessary in order to enable them to construct. So far as smelters are concerned, these people will have power only to buy the same as any individual.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Smith), as he comes from British Ccl'unbia, should know more about this
industry than people who live at a distance from the mining regions. It appears to me that by allowing that clause to go into the charter, if there is any independent smelter in British Columbia, it will place them at the mercy of the Canadian Pacific Railway corporation. That corporation is' practically the only carrier in that country, and having control'of all the carrying trade, they will be able to build smelters of their own, and cut down the prices to such an extent that an independent smelter could not live.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We have got one smelter at Grand Forks and one at Nelson, both independent and private smelters. I have yet to hear the first objection ever made in British Columbia with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway owning the Trail smelter. I think we all regard it as one of the best things the Canadian Pacific Railway ever did for British Columbia when they became owners of that smelter.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I did not wish to say they have done this in the past, but I say that in the future, if they want to exercise the power that is given them under that proposition, they can freeze out any independent smelting industry in British Columbia.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to what appears to me a doubt about section 11, which says that the company shall have powers for the expropriation of land.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: All the expropriation clauses have been struck out.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The point in my mind did not arise from the absence of those words, but there was a question whether the expropriation powers would not inherently apply to purposes which you made part of the railway undertaking without an expressed provision that they should apply.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The object of putting in the expropriation clause there was to give them that power, but the committee struck it out on the understanding that the clauses of the General Railway Act should apply which only gives them special powers. But none of these are in the general powers of the Railway Aqt.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I accept the hon. gentleman's statement, but I was referring to the remark made by the hon. member for Lanark that the House was so impressed with the doubt that they put in the negative words, that these powers should not apply to the purposes of the undertaking.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROW HEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Some members raised the point whether some of these Acts did not give powers for expropriating for the purposes mentioned in that clause.

House in committee on Bill (No. Cl) respecting W. C. Edwards Company (Limited).-Mr. Rosamond.
On the preamble,

I think it fair to call the attention of the committee to the departure which has been made in this Bill and in the Bill next following, from the practice that has hitherto prevailed. It may be all right, and probably the committee may approve of it, but I think it my duty to call their attention to it. The original charter of the W. C. Edwards Company (Limited) enabled them to acquire, hold and deal with the shares of any boom or river improvement company, and the new addition to the Act which we now have before us, provided that they should not only have that power but they should also have power to acquire, hold, deal with and dispose of the shares in any other company any of whose powers were within the scope of this company incorporated. Now, in the Bills introduced in the Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee there is no limitation of the powers given to companies at all. Industrial companies have omnibus powers, and so the effect of this Bill now before us is to give this company or any other company power to deal with the shares of all industrial companies of any kind or description. That may be good or bad policy, but it is an entire departure from the policy adopted heretofore. There were objections taken in the Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee, and a restriction was adopted to the effect that the powers shall not be exercised unless the shareholders at a special meeting authorize it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I think it is the duty of the government to have some policy with reference to this matter, and to lead the House in the direction in which they think we should go in regard to private Bill legislation. If the clause is so objectionable as the minister says it is, he should announce the policy of the government in reference to it. The clauses which are in

this Bill are precisely the same, and give no greater powers than the clauses we have adopted in preceding Bills. If they are objectionable, and I think perhaps there is some foundation for the statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, he should be in a position to guide the House.

My hon. friend is asking me to go a little further than any minister ever attempted to do before. This is private Bill legislation, I spoke as a member of the Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee. Personally I thought it was a mistake to take this new departure, but a majority of the committee thought differently, they did take this departure. The government has no special policy in the matter, it is a matter for the House to determine as they please. But I thought it my duty to call the attention of the committee to the departure which the Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee recommended ; having done that, I have discharged my duty. I have not stated any serious objection to it. My objection taken in the committee was this, that under the new legislation which we have adopted, a company might be incorporated for lumbering purposes, and buy a controlling interest in every industrial company in Canada. That was my objection. It did not prevail in the Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee. The committee, by a large majority, thought I was wrong, but the government had no policy in the matter. It was only my own individual opinion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This is a new doctrine which is laid down by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies). The government of the day are responsible for all legislation that goes through the House, and if a Bill is going through this House prejudicial to the public interest it is the duty of the government to protect the public interest. But, the Liberal government do not believe in that. They are abandoning the protection of the public interest, not only here but at Toronto, and in every other legislature in which they have a majority. We intends to hold the government responsible. As to this particular measure I have no opinion of my own but the doctrine laid down by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that the government are not responsible for private legislation that goes through the House, and that it is not the duty of the government to protect Die public interest is a bad doctrine that Should never be enunciated by a government that made such professions as this government have made.

My hon. friend is altogether mistaken. I never laid down the doctrine that it was not the duty of the government to protect the public interest.

Mr, MACLEAN. The hon. gentleman says he has no opinion in regard to the public interest.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I merely thought 1 was discharging my duty in calling the attention of this committee to the fact that there had been a departure from the practice hitherto adopted in tho Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee. That departure I did not approve of. A large majority of the committee did approve of it, and the government did not take any part in the matter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: You should have.
The government is not going to take part in every bit of private legislation that goes through the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The government must protect the public interest.
The moment the amendment was adopted that this power should not be exercised until two-thirds of the shareholders approved of it I said no more.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I think that it is a matter of public interest. We are changing entirely the direction of private legislation. This is not a matter of indifference. We are deciding the question as to whether industrial companies can go into any business at all connected with their original enterprise and we have already decided that railway companies can go into mining and lumbering when it is necessary to carry on their enterprise. My own personal opinion is favourable to this particular Bill, but I think this is a point upon which we ought to have the policy of the government. It is a very grave innovation. It is something entirely new as the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies) has said. It touches the public policy of the country and we are entitled) to know what the position of the government is in view of future questions of this kind that may arise.

The policy of the government is that it is not going to interfere with the action of the House on a Bill of this kind at all, but to let the committee of this House adopt the amendment or reject it as it pleases. It is not a matter so important or grave that a public policy should be adopted and pronounced upon it. It is simply a departure from the practice of the Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee. The committee have never given to industrial companies the right to deal in the shares of other companies. You have provided in the statute law of the country what the policy of the country is on that question. So far as loan companies are concerned they are not permitted to deal in the shares
of other companies, so far as banks are concerned they are not permitted to deal in the shares of other banks, and so far as industrial companies are concerned they are not permitted to deal in the shares of other companies unless the special Act of incorporation gives them that power. In this case the special Act of incorporation gives them that power with the limitation that two-thirds of the shareholders must approve of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The other day, in Quebec, the city of Montreal was raided of a lot of its rights by a powerful corporation there. When the Prime Minister of Quebec was called to account, all he had to say was : I did not know such a Bill was going through, but at the next session of legislature I may repeal it, or I may call a special session to repeal it. Ho abandoned the public interest. He was there to protect the municipal rights of Montreal for the protection of which the government were responsible. It was a confession of weakness on their part that they did not protect the public interest. The same doctrine is being laid down here to-night by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
