I have heard it discussed several times since I have had the honour of a seat in this. House and every time I have noticed that there has been an increase in the intensity of interest manifested in the study of the question. I. may add that I think it fortunate that he has been upheld in the view which he laid before the House by the hon. member for St. Antoine division (Mr. COMMONS
Roddick), who represents, I tliink, tlie most important, or if not, one of tlie most important constituencies in tiiis Dominion, one deeply interested in the question of transportation. I may also add that for my part I listened to liim, as I am sure did many other lion, members of this House, with particular pleasure when he treated the phase of the question which concerns the hydrographic survey, a subject upon which his high scientific qualifications entitle him to speak with authority. But, as soon as these two hon. gentlemen had spoken, we had proof of a divergence of views amongst hon. members of this House. We heard one hon. gentleman who sits on the foremost seat on the opposite side of the House express his dissent from the views and from the doctrines expressed by the two hon. gentlemen who had preceded' him. We heard, Sir, an hon. minister of the Crown, the hon. member for Quebec West (Hon. Mr. Dobell) take exception in very formal terms to the proposition that we should expend any more money in deepening, and, as far as I could understand, improving the navigation of the St. Lawrence above the city of Quebec. I have no doubt that before this debate is closed we will hear other opinions diverging equally from the opinions to which I have just referred, But, Sir, let us remember that while we have been discussing and examining this question with very little practical result during the past five or six years the enemy is really at our doors. We have to the south of us a population with whom it is very difficult for us to compete, men of immense practical ability, of untiring ambition, of immense wealth, having control of untold financial resources who are acting while we are speaking, and I venture to say that the proportion of the western trade which we are so desirous of securing and of which we have such a small percentage at the present moment, will gradually diminish and dwindle to nothing unless we pass from words to deeds and unless we take active steps and that as soon as possible to secure a far larger proportion of that trade. I venture the opinion that in the face of the rivals against whom we have to cope, if we had not the assistance of nature the struggle to which the hon. member (Mr. Bickerdike) has invited us would be almost hopeless. Not only in the United States but all over the world we find rivals in trade, and these countries have given the question of transportation far more intelligent study and practical application and with far greater effective results than has Canada. Look at the Argentine Republic. Look at the admirable manner in which they have progressed towards the solution of this transportation question. Have not our cousins at the antipodes, the New Zealanders and the Australians, have they not reached a far more advanced stage in the solution of this question than we have. It is only a night or two ago than in strains

of great, and as I think unjustified self-laudation-I say it without giving to this question in any sense a political colour, because it has none-we heard the Minister of Agriculture, when he asked us to vote $140,000 for cold storage, declaring that that question was in a satisfactory condition. That hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fisher) who a few days ago refused to classify even a tomato, is apparently very ignorant of what is being done in those countries to which I have referred. And when I asked the Minister of Agriculture whether in our contracts with the ship-owners we had secured such a low degree of temperature as zero, that homy handed minister informed me that I knew nothing about the question, and he ventured the assertion, clearly unfounded, that a temperature of 29 or 30 degrees was all that was required for the transportation of meats. If that hon. minister will look at the New Zealand yearbook which my hon. and esteemed friend from Victoria (Mr. Ross) placed upon the Table of this House, and if he looks at an article in this paper on the New Zealand frozen mutton trade, he will find that no temperature less than eight degrees above zero is tolerated in that trade. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) was entirely mistaken, and when the New Zealander referred to by Macaulay crosses the seas, he will, I fear, find something else to sketch than the broken arches of London bridge.
But, Sir. to return to this question upon which I wish to be as brief as possible, I venture the assertion that we must without any delay whatever apply ourselves to its solution if we wish to get any practical results, and to secure that share of the immense western traffic to which we are entitled. First and foremost, we must free the canals. This will involve considerable sacrifice on our part. It will involve a loss of revenue of some $200,000 a year, but we must be prepared not only to bend our intellectual resources towards the study of this question, but we' must put our hands in our pockets and make large financial sacrifices if we are to succeed. We must free the canals. For my part I believe, as I am sure many of the members of the House do, that there is a great deal to be said in favour of the Georgian Bay canal scheme, which has been so often discussed and towards the accomplishment of which so very little has been done. I believe that canal will develop to an immense degree that portion of the country which is now called New Ontario, and in which there are immense natural resources. It will shorten by three hundred miles the route from the west to the seaboard.
Three hundred and eighty-seven miles.

Three hundred and eighty-seven miles as my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) remarks. I believe, Sir, that there

will be in the future sufficient trade to make that waterway remunerative, while at the same time no injury will be done to the existing canals. Then after the canals, we have the port of Montreal to consider, and it seems to me that the port of Montreal should be properly equipped without any delay whatever. I have understood it to be the sense of this House in the last parliament, that Montreal was to be considered our national port, as it should be. I did not understand from any of the remarks of my hon. friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Bicker-dike) or my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Roddick) that there was any idea to discriminate against Quebec. I believe with the hon. gentleman from Quebec West (Hon. Mr. Dobell) that there is a great future in store for the port of Quebec. It ihas a splendid harbour and a great back country : there is a great country to the south of Quebec with vast agricultural resources, and I have no doubt that the port of Quebec will continue to grow in importance. It must remain an important port at any rate, if that city becomes the garrison town contemplated and sighed for by my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Chariton). But. Sir, we must not forget that Montreal is at the head of ocean navigation, that it has an immense shipping trade at the present time, the largest in the country, and without insisting too much upon the admitted principle that the further ships penetrate inland, the cheaper the transportation, we have always considered that Montreal was entitled to national support as the national outlet for our products. At the present time the harbour improvement works at Montreal proceed too slowly. Why is it that there has been so much delay. I ventured the opinion the other day that the transportation question was too great a one to be confined to the intellectual resources, however great they may be, of a single man. At Montreal we encountered this difficulty. We have to deal with the harbour commissioners ; we have to deal with the Minister of Public Works ; we haw to deal with the Minister of Marine as regards lights and signals in the river ; we have to deal with the Customs Department, and we have to deal with the Department of Railways and Canals. I state here that if the improvements in the port of Montreal have not advanced more rapidly, the delay is due in a large measure to the divided authority of these different bodies to which I have referred. I have no hesitation also in saying that the delay is due in great part to clashing between the members of the government, possibly between the Minister of Public Works and some of his colleagues, and, clashing with the harbour board of Montreal. There has been clashing-the Minister of Public Works will not deny it- between himself and the harbour board in respect to these improvements and the way they ought to be carried out. The min102
ister does not deny it, and we have the proof that there is not complete accord in the government on the matter. How can we expect to make the port of Montreal what it should be, a port capable of competing with the great American ports, if we have, among the parties upon whom rests the responsibility of carrying out those improvements and placing that port upon the proper footing, such clashing as I have alluded to.
I have no hesitation in saying, for my own part, that if the Minister of Public Works had been alone concerned with those improvements, whatever might be said against some of his ideas or some of the plans he approved of, there would have been quicker progress; we would not have that port in the unsatisfactory condition in which it stands to-day; and we would not have- what is to my mind, grave as it is in itself, merely an indication of what is going on everywhere-the business of the Grand Trunk Railway transferred from Montreal to Portland. I do not blame that company. We have benefited the Grand Trunk Railway Company extraordinarily. We have conferred upon it, in connection with the H-olongation of the Intercolonial to Montreal, great favours; but we have not provided for what might have been anticipated; and the consequence is that the managers of that company, who were bound first and foremost to look to the interests of the shareholders, finding the port of Montreal an impossible port, felt it necessary to go to a country where greater facilities are afforded. Let me give you an instance. It is a well-known fact, for it has been tested, that the capacity at Montreal for moving grain is
4,000	bushels an hour or thereabouts, whereas at Duluth grain is moved at the rate of over 195,000 bushels in 155 minutes; and we cannot doubt that at the American seaboard there are equal facilities. In view of the existing state of things at Montreal, and the dangers of navigation and the high rates for insurance and freight below Montreal, there is no reason for astonishment if we find our share of the carrying trade removed to the neighbouring country. And, Sir, as evidencing the application to" the solution of this important question of the homely saying that too many cooks spoil the soup, and that there are too many charged with the solution of this question-some who have not the knowledge and others who have not the time-one of the principal accusations brought by the organ of the Minister of Public Works was precisely that clashing between the ideas of the Minister of Public Works and the ideas of other people holding control over that port. This is what La Patrie, in its article of the 2nd of April, says :
As soon as the Liberal party in 1S96-7 arrived in power, Mr. Laurier and his colleagues immediately set to work to study the question of the improvement of the port of Montreal; and



Mr. Tarte particularly brought to this problem a zeal, an energy, and an intelligence which everybody recognizes in him. Nevertheless, since four years, the efforts of the Minister of Public Works have invariably been stopped by the Tories on the harbour board and by certain Conservative organs of the opposition.
What those organs are, I do not know.
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. I have nothing to do with that article.

Does the non. minister disown this statement of the case ?
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. Well, I believe there is a great deal of exaggeration in that article.

There may be; bnt still the very words of the minister uphold my proposition that there are too many concerned in the solution of this question. Further on, the article says :
We would now have vast grain elevators in Montreal if the opposition, helped by a portion
of the harbour board

The document should be examined by any member of the House who takes any interest in the question. In an interview with the underwriters in which I bad the advantage of assisting, the government stated that if the improvements-and they are not so very costly-suggested by that deputation were made, inevitably the rates of insurance would go down.
Now, one word more and I have finished. There is no doubt when we come to this question of transportation, we must be prepared for some sacrifice of money. I believe, however, after the experience I have had on the floor of this House, that we must be prepared to bring to bear upon our ordinary annual expenditure, a greater degree of caution and a determination to pare off a great deal of useless expenditure. We voted last night, If I mistake not, $125,000 for the maintenance of these buildings which surround us. 1 ventured the opinion then, and I hold it still that that is a greatly exaggerated expenditure, and if we were to adopt a proper system we could reduce that by at least half. The same remark applies to a great deal of expenditure that we make annually. In regard to local improvements also, we were engaged last night in voting large sums for minor local works calculated, I venture to say, mainly to satisfy local demands for public buildings, for breakwaters, for wharfs, and so on, in certain counties. I am not prepared to deny that these works are of use, though I question very much whether, in the majority of cases, they are useful in proportion to the amount voted. But, important as these works may be, we must be prepared in the face of the urgency of this question to curtail these expenditures. We must educate public opinion to understand that, in the case, for instance, of a public building, people must be patient and we must be prepared to vote a larger amount of money to the solution of a question which is of interest to the country at large. In my own county-and no doubt the same is true of many other constituencies-there are a large Mr. MONK.
number of public works that would be useful. But, useful as they might be locally they would be of no use as compared with the immense general benefit which would be derived from a large or at any rate a sufficient expenditure for the solution of this question. Sir, 1 believe that if the question is examined as it should be, and if proper propositions are made to us by the government in the direction of its solution on this side of the House, there will be no opposition to anything that would put us in a position to compete properly with our American neighbour. And I believe that the hon. minister without portfolio (Mr. Dobell) should do a little more than what he told us of this afternoon. We have not only to develop a great system of transportation here, but it is time and high time 1 venture to say that this government should give its attention to the fast Atlantic service. For instance, whatever may be said, and whatever we may do to improve the carrying trade from the west to the seaboard, unless that question of a fast Atlantic service has prompt and effective attention, we shall still remain behind our American neighbours and our other competitors.

I can unite with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) very heartily in saying that the question now under discussion is one of very great importance to Canada. The subject of the selection of the best ocean port is a matter that relates very intimately to our success in the carrying' trade; and the relative advantages of Quebec, Montreal and other ports should receive careful consideration. The decision arrived at with reference to the matter will be one of very great moment to this Dominion. The discussion upon the question so far, has been with the exception of one speaker engaged in by what, perhaps, may be properly termed special advocates of the respective interests of two great seaports. The claims of Montreal have been very ably presented by my hon. friend from the St. Lawrence division (Mr. Bickerdike), the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Roddick) and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). The claims for Quebec have been presented by a member of the Privy Council (Hon. Mr. Dobell). I rise now as an impartial observer without the slightest local prejudice or feeling with regard to this matter to present certain views to this House with reference to this question which strikes me as having pertinence and force. It is true that, if Montreal is the proper ocean port for this Dominion, large appropriations should be made. It is true that the character of that port, the appliances for the handling of business should be made more efficient; and, if it is to be the great entrepot of Canadian commerce, no time should be lost in placing the port in a position that my hon. friend from Jacques

Cartier (Mr. Monk) urged tliat it should be placed in. If, on tlie contrary, Montreal is not the most eligible and advantageous point for seeking to centre the seaboard business for this Dominion, then, whatever point may be selected should receive due and efficient attention from this government. It strikes me, in listening to this debate, that the advocates of the claims of Montreal have unconsciously perhaps, but in a most powerful manner presented to this House the disadvantages of that port and the difficulties under which it labours. I have not heard anybody refer to the advantages of Quebec, but those advantages, so far as the port itself is concerned, are self-evident. Quebec is properly at the head of ocean navigation. Quebec has unlimited facilities for the transaction of business. It has a magnificent anchorage, it has room for the navies of the world, it has room for wharfs, and docks, and warehouses without limit, to an extent to accommodate if necessary the commerce of this entire continent. It has always surprised me that the natural advantages of Quebec had not secured for that port greater consideration than it has received. I do not desire by any means to take a position here as an advocate of either of these great seaports. My feelings are exactly the same towards the one as the other. They are both splendid cities, with magnificent natural features, two of the finest points on this continent. My best ' wishes go out to each of them, but as a Canadian, I desire to consider what in the interest of the whole country is the proper course to pursue with regard to the selection of the port which is to be considered and made, so far as the Dominion government can make it, the port of the Dominion.
Now, my hon. friend from St. Lawrence division told us this afternoon that when the St. Lawrence canals were completed Montreal would handle 100,000.000 bushels of American grain ; and when the Georgian Bay canal is completed Montreal would handle 300,000,000 bushels of American grain. He reminded me of rather an optimistic estimate made in this House some years ago by Sir Charles Tupper, who estimated that about the present date there would be 040.000,000 bushels of wheat raised in the Canadian North-west. These calculations as to the prospective growth of business are always somewhat unreliable, and it is not well to pay too much attention to them.
We have to consider in the first place the relative advantages and the relative disadvantages of the various routes that are seeking to obtain the trade of the great west. As my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has said, the competition in this respect is exceedingly keen, and he pointed to the fact that our neighbours to the south of us have command of unlimited amounts of capital, have great industrial energy, and are using their utmost efforts
to secure this trade. Well, the truth is that they are enjoying the great bulk of this trade, and have been doing so for many years past. Montreal. I believe, has never received more than 15 per cent of the western trade, and the question for us to consider now is how shall we make inroads upon this trade, and how shall we divert from American channels a percentage of the commerce that they now enjoy.
Now, at the outset, if we are to make a fair consideration of this question, we will find that the advantages possessed by American routes are very great. In the first place, they all terminate at seaports that are open summer and winter, in which the channels of communication are open for a somewhat longer time than our own channels of communication by water. Buffalo, at the foot of the great lakes, receives all the grain from the whole enormous coast of six great inland seas, at freight rates, as a rule, not above 2 cents per bushel. From Buffalo grain can be transported to New York at a very low rate. It is said to be a fact that the New York Central road can carry grain from Buffalo to New York for 50 cents a ton, or 24 cents per hundred, and leave a tolerably fair margin for profits. If this is the case, with freights of one and a quarter and one and a half, seldom more than one and three-quarter cents, per bushel from Duluth, or Chicago, to Buffalo, and 'with these low rates to the port of New York where grain reaches a point where the port is open summer and winter, where there is always a great supply of vessels, where ocean freights are lower than from Montreal, where insurance is lower, where everything makes to the advantage of that port, I say under these conditions we have got a herculean task before us to secure any considerable portion of that trade. It becomes, therefore, all the more necessary carefully to consider the best methods for doing this thing, and the best port to select, to consider what are the means we should mse for the purpose of securing the trade we desire to secure.
Now, we are told that we want the Georgian Bay canal. Well, the Georgian Bay canal would be a desirable thing, the Georgian Bay canal would serve many useful purposes, but I am very doubtful whether it would to any considerable extent reduce the cost of freight upon grain from the western lakes to the Canadian seaboard. A year ago the Booth road transported 11.000,000 bushels of wheat from Depot Harbour to Montreal, and a great portion of that wheat was carried from Chicago or from Duluth to Montreal for three and three-quarter cents per bushel. Now, to what extent are you likely to reduce that cost of transportation by the construction of the Georgian Bay canal ? This Booth road could lay that wheat down in Quebec for just a trifle more perhaps, a quarter or half a cent a bushel more, than they charge for laying it

down in Montreal, namely, three and three-quarter cents. You cannot reduce that cost of transportation materially by the construction of the Georgian Bay canal.
In making our calculations and considering the advantages likely to be derived from the construction of this canal, it would be well for us to take advantage of the investigations that have been made on the other side of the line. There has been a question for several years as to wliat kind of waterway would best serve the purpose of carrying grain from the great lakes to the seaboard. There have been advocates of a 25-foot channel, there have been advocates of a 21-foot channel, and a 20-foot channel. There was a report made by Major Symons, of the engineer corps, United States army, who went into this question most carefully, and his decision was that the cheapest possible method of communication and of carriage of freight from the great lakes to the seaboard was by means of a canal from Buffalo to New York, with a 10-foot draught and with barges of from 1.000 to 1,200 tons burden. He pointed out that in a canal with a 21-foot draught, a vessel which brought a cargo down the lakes, would necessarily go through that canal at a low rate of speed, and would have to keep on hand her entire crew of engineers, firemen, and so forth ; and that she would go to Xew York, take tin her cargo and come back by the same slow method through the canal, and could not have a speed of over three or four miles an hour. The result of his careful calculation was that the cost of freight upon grain by the barge system would be less than by a ship canal of 21 feet, with vessels calculated to carry grain from Chicago or Duluth without breaking bulk. The state of New York, after considering all the data possible bearing upon this question, are taking measures to appropriate $26,000,000 to construct a barge canal from Buffalo to Albany with a branch to Oswego, with a draught of ten feet, and with large locks to accommodate barges of 1,000 tons burden. They believe, whether rightly or wrongly, that this is the cheapest possible mode of the transportation of grain from the lakes to the seaboard, and will answer the purpose better than a ship canal.
Now, if that is the case the Georgian Bay canal would hardly serve the purpose that we anticipate. There is another thing to be taken into consideration. Within the last twenty years the cost of transportation by rail has been reduced two-thirds by the introduction of the heavy steel rail, the fishplate joint, lower grades, air-brakes, and engines that will haul forty cars carrying fifty tons in a car, instead of hauling twenty ears with a load of ten tons to the cnr. This improvement in the method of railway transportation is going on. We have not reached the end of it yet. We have not arrived at the point where we have attained all that can be attained in the matter of transportation Mr. CHARLTON.
by rail. I venture to say that to-day the Georgian Bay canal would not be capable of competing with the Booth line of railway in taking grain from the lakes to Montreal or Quebec, and that in ten years the Booth line of railway and other lines of railways, by the improvements that are in progress, will have reduced the cost of moving freight upon their lines by possibly one-half what it is to-day. I think we may dismiss the idea of spending $100,000,000 on the Georgian Bay canal, for the present, at least, and that we may continue the use of the means that we have now, either by our railway system or our canal system, of laying grain down at the seaboard.
Now, we have to take into consideration : What is the best method of diverting this American trade ? How are we to get it, and where are we to place it for transhipment to ocean vessels ? The hon. member for St. Lawrence division, Montreal (Mr. Bielcerdike) asked me, this afternoon, when I first discovered that Quebec had advantages superior to those of Montreal. I had been a member of this House for a great many years, and 1 had never discovered this till quite recently, and he rather suspected that I had made use of this statement for the purpose of squaring myself with Quebec because some time last summer I had said that it would be a good idea, for ethnic and social reasons, to bring the races into contact by having a garrison and a large city there. When the St. Lawrence canals were deepened to 14 feet, the whole problem was changed. Before these canals were deepened bulk had to be broken at Kingston, and grain sent from Lake Ontario to Montreal on barges of 0 feet draught. When the canals were completed to a depth of 14 feet, you had navigation from Port Colborne on Lake Erie to Montreal for vessels of 14 feet draught, and the necessity of transhipment at Kingston, and the increased cost of freight in consequence of putting the grain upon a small class of barges, passed away. Now. you have, since the enlargement of these canals, an invitation to a class of upper lake shipping that is thrown out of business, a class of vessels that draw 14 feet of water, that are not unable to compete with the new class of vessels of 5,000 and 6,000 tons that are bringing down grain from Chicago and Duluth to Buffalo for a cent and a quarter a bushel-you have an invitation to these vessels which will crowd into this trade, and which, when the improvements at Port Colborne harbour are completed so as to allow large vessels from the upper lakes to come in. will take their cargoes at that harbour and carry them direct through to the St. Lawrence. The question is : Where should they deliver them ? Y*ou have an unlimited amount of tonnage. There are hundreds of these vessels that cannot work profitably between Duluth, or Chicago, and Buffalo, that would be glad to go into this

trade, and the question is : Will these vessels tranship that grain to the ocean vessels at Montreal or at Quebec, and what will be the advantage in the case it is done at Quebec over the advantage of doing the business at Montreal ? Now, these vessels can go down to Quebec without having a channel 30 feet deep and 000 feet wide. They can go down there with the present channel. They can go down if the channel filled up and they only had the average depth of the water of Lake St. Peter. They can go to Quebec and deliver that grain at an inappreciable fraction of a cent above the cost of doing it at Montreal, and they can meet at Quebec any vessel that sails the seas. A steamer of 20,000 tons can come there, cast her anchor in mid-stream and ride safely at anchor. She can go to the docks and have 50 feet of water. There are unlimited facilities for transacting the business, and business can be made to centre at Quebec. The cost of transportation from the lakes to Quebec will be practically the same as it is to Montreal and vessels can go there of any capacity, and they can go there, if they cannot maintain business for the year round, a month earlier than they can go to Montreal, and they can go from Quebec two months later in the season than they can go from Montreal. These are the advantages. No ?4,COO,000 of expense in dredging the bottom of Lake St. Peter, no money to be expended to raise wharfs so that sheds will not be swept off when the ice shove comes, no money to be expended for the purpose of getting places where you will have room to pile lumber, no money to be expended to make provision that butter, cheese, flour and wheat will not spoil, and cattle will not deteriorate in value $4 or $5 per head. All these things you have at Quebec. You have facilities for doing business without cost, or relatively without cost, and you can save the enormous expenditure of money that will be required to improve the port of Montreal, and have ber-ter facilities and a better port than you can got at Montreal iby the expenditure of any amount of money you please to put into it. Right along from Cape Diamond up the river for five miles from Quebec, are the old timber coves ; five miles where you can have docks for the whole distance, if you desire it, for handling the lumber that you have, not room in Montreal to handle, dockage on the other side of the river, dockage up the river for five miles, for ten miles, if you choose, and a safe au-chorage in mid-stream for the entire distance. And finally, you have a port that is not excelled in the world. Greater natural advantages are not possessed by any other port in the world. We can reach this port as cheaply as we can reach Montreal, we can get there without any great expenditure of money, we can keep the port open two or three months longer than we can keep the port at Montreal open, and for all these
reasons, it seems to me that the interests of Canada at large will be served by making or attempting to make the city of Quebec the great commercial centre of the Dominion. It has natural facilities. It has access to the ocean. Nature has designed it for the purposes that I am laying before the House, while Montreal is a point, where, if you attempt to make it an ocean port, you will contend for all time with difficulties. If you have a channel 30 feet deep and 000 feet wide you will draw down the water from above and create dangers by reason of the current, and when you have done that, you will have a narrow channel that is dangerous for a great ocean-going steamer to attempt' to navigate. With a stiff wind blowing across the river it requires very fine seamanship to keep such a vessel from drifting on the mud. The difficulties connected with navigation between Montreal and Quebec are mainly the reason for the high insurance rates, and must inevitably increase freight rates, and put a damper upon the commercial business of the port. That is the view I take of this matter.
I believe that we are working against na ture in going past one of the finest seaports in the world, a seaport which has 100 feet of water in mid-channel and can have 40 or 50 feet of water at the docks close to shore, a seaport with an anchorage sufficient to accommodate all the navies of the world, and with access to the ocean three months longer than from Montreal. I believe we are working against nature in striving to force business past that natural port, away up the river through a ditch dug in Lake St. Peter, to the city of Montreal, 180 miles above. I think we had better let these lake vessels that will carry the grain from Port Colborne, where vessels can come from up the lakes drawing 21 feet of water ; we had better let the vesselg to which the grain is transferred at that point proceed on their voyage to Quebec and transfer their cargoes there at a cost oif perhaps one-tenth of a cent a bushel more than it would cost in the city of Montreal.

We will not stop them in Montreal if they want to go.
Mr: CHARLTON. You cannot stop them in Montreal, when natural conditions assert themselves. Quebec is going to assert herself. The natural advantages of Quebec cannot be overridden. We are going to have a garrison there, and an English nopu-lation there, and the centre of the business of the country there, and we are going to see ethnic and social conditions there that will work a revolution in Quebec and make it the great export city of this Dominion.
And make them loyal.
They are loyal now, and we will make them rich and give them business.
I am afraid the garrison is coming to Montreal.

I think perhaps commerce will come to Quebec before the garrison, and I would rather see it so. I agree with some of the contentions made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). We want free canals ; we want free ports. We want a free port at Montreal. We want a free port at Quebec. We do not want to have any burdens placed upon the commerce of this country that can be removed, and we have to remove these burdens if we are going to compete with our rivals to the south of the line. That is perfectly apparent. Let these burdens be removed. Take off the tolls on the canals ; take off the port charges, and make both ports and canals free. And with regard to the hydrographic survey, by all means let the Department of Marine expend the money necessary to make a thorough survey of every foot of that river from Montreal to the Gulf
The survey is being made between Montreal and Quebec now.

All right, let it be proceeded with. Let us have a thorough hydrographic survey by the Belle Isle and by the other route, and let us have no more of such complaints, as my hon. friend (Mr. Roddick) presented to the House from British naval officers and British ship-masters as to the lack of information, and the misleading character of some of the information at their command with regard to this great waterway.
The ^ MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES. ^ ou have now a perfect hydrographic survey of the Straits of Belle Isle, and the complaints of the British officer referred to were made years ago. The British government have been engaged for twenty years completing that hydrographic survey.

It is most gratifying to know this, and if there is anything lacking in that respect let it be supplied at once. My hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Edwards) informed us that we were not in a condition which would enable us to carry on commerce successfully because we had not an import trade, and the hon. gentleman from East York (Mr. Maclean) asked him how we compared in that respect with the United States. I was led to infer from the statement of the hon. member (Mr. Edwards) that we in Canada imported less per capita than they did in the United States. I find from the Trade and Navigation Returns, that our imports last year amounted to $180.0(10,0(10, which represents about $32 per head of our population. I have not the Mr. BICKERDIKE.
American statistics at hand, but taking the population at 73,000,000, if the United States imported per capita as much as we do, they would have imported $2,400,000,000, which is probably $400,000,000 more than their entire import and export trade. If 1 am not mistaken our import trade per capita is about two and a half times as great as that of the United States. Whatever may be our advantages or lack of advantages with regard to return cargoes, I do not think that we get as small a proportion of return cargoes, on this basis, as they do in the United States.
1 again desire to disclaim any intention or desire to advocate the interests of one point to the detriment of another. I endeavour to look at this question from the standpoint of a person interested in the general welfare of the Dominion. We have vast interests here to protect; we have a great future before us, and we want to avail ourselves of the very best methods of protecting aud advancing our interests. And while great interests are centred in Montreal and will continue to centre there, I think the views I have placed before the House with regard to the superior commercial advantages of Quebec are just and well founded. While I would not think for a moment of counselling the adoption of a policy that would leave Montreal side-tracked or leave that city without the means to maintain its port in good order, yet I think we may as well contemplate the propriety and necessity of making the natural seaport of this Dominion the point where our commerce from the west shall centre. We ought to direct some great railway to Quebec. Quebec is almost as near the wheat fields of the west as Montreal if a proper railway line is selected. Quebec is the natural point from which to tap James Bay. The province of Quebec has a vast area in the interior, of land yet to open for cultivation which will support millions of inhabitants, and I am happy to believe, Sir, that the forecast I have made, with regard to the future greatness of Quebec will be realized ; that the natural advantages of Quebec will command that prosperity which it is entitled to and which it will be sure to receive. I have arrived at this conclusion partly from the fact that I have been upon the ground ; have made a study of the matter ; have realized after personal observation the advantages that city possesses.
Dear old Quebec.

Fine old city. An historic city. A city that had a history when there was not a white man in this vast region of the great lakes, and not a white man in the Mississippi valley. Quebec was then a city of importance and I believe it will rise to its pristine greatness again. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we should dismiss from our minds the prejudices that are engendered of local strifes and local jealous-

ies, that we should look on this matter from the broad national standpoint and realize that if we are to secure for ourselves that share of the carrying trade from the west which we desire ; if we are to pluck from the hands of these American lines anything more than the paltry 10 or 12 per cent of the business which we enjoy now, we have to make diligent and energetic use of all the means and all the advantages that nature has given us, aud amongst these is to avail ourselves of the port of Quebec, one of the best seaports in the world.

Mr. Speaker, as one of the representatives from the city of Montreal in this parliament. I feel it my duty to offer a few remarks on the question now before the House. It shall be necessary for me to answer the hon. membei for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) on certain points, and to deal also, with some of the observations which have been addressed to the House by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards), and by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). It is, I believe, the object of every member from the district of Montreal-whether he represents the city proper or an adjoining constituency-to treat this trade question in a broad and national basis and not as affecting the city of Montreal alone. I shall treat this question as a question of the national route of the St. Lawrence and as affecting the trade of the whole country-
But before discussing the question itself, let me at ouce take up the position of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, which has been assailed by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).' The Harbour Commission of Montreal is not a new institution of this government. It is a very old institution, dating back for about forty years, and it has been maintained by succeeding governments during that time. It has been maintained in spite of attacks upon it and in spite of periodical demands for its abolition and the substitution of the administration of the Department of Public Works. I do not want to pronounce upon that question, although I have my own views upon it; but on a large and broad question like this, I do not want to press my personal views at all. Some hon. members of this House may not know that the Harbour Commission of Montreal is composed of eleven persons, of whom six are chosen by the Governor in Council and five by the five most important public bodies of the city of Montreal-one by the shipping interest, one by the corn exchange, one by the Board of Trade, one by the Chambre du Commerce, one by the City Council. In this way the different public bodies, those who know something about the trade aud commerce of the port, are supposed to be represented on the harbour commission. This is not the first time that the harbour commission has been assailed
not only in this House, but also outside; but I think my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier will admit that it was assailed a great deal more some years ago than it has been since 1890.

I did not assail it. I said there was a division of authority between the harbour board, the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and I suggested the appointment of a commission. But I never had it in my mind to assail the harbour board at all, and I did not do so.

If I understood the words of my hon. friend, they meant that the Harbour Commission of Montreal were rather slow-that they were moving too slowly altogether; and I presumed when he used those words that he was assailing the present harbour board. I want to answer that part of my hon. friend's remarks. The present Harbour Board of Montreal has existed since the end of the year 1897. It really went into office in 1898. Let us see what it has accomplished since that time. Since the year 1889, the old Harbour Commissioners of Montreal had been fighting together over a plan of improvements of the harbour. In 1889, $1,000,090 had been voted by the city of Montreal to help that commission to do certain works which were considered absolutely necessary to protect the city against inundation aud to provide accommodation for the export trade of the whole Dominion. From 1889 to 1S98 they had been fighting among themselves; they had not agreed upon any settled plan for making the improvements really needed; and only part of the work had been completed-the guard pier in the centre of the St. Lawrence. In 1898, as soon as the present board came in charge of the affairs of tlie harbour, they proceeded at once to have those plans adopted, and they were adopted in June of that year, and were approved by the Department of Public Works. It did not take them ten years or nine years to do this. In five months they got the plans adopted, and they at once proceeded with the works. After starting the works according to those plans, what did they discover ? They discovered that the estimates made by the engineer were below the amount that was needed to make the improvements. They at ouce came before this government and asked for legislation which would enable them to borrow enough money to go on with the improvements in accordance with the accepted plan. This government did not hesitate a moment. In the session of 189S, the necessary legislation was granted, under which the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal were authorized to borrow $3,000,000 to go on witli those improvements. Of course, the contracts had not been given out to a large extent previous to the season of 1898. and I will admit that the works did not proceed during that season as fast as they would have

bour commissioners at Montreal are erecting wliarfs on the high level to provide against inundation. Permanent warehouses will be arranged, which will reduce the cost of handling the freight in the port. All these things, of course, cannot be done in a day. The harbour commissioners do not rent to any company the right to run cars on the wharfs, but the roads belong to the harbour commissioners themselves, and the use of the roads is open to all the railways on paying a certain rental. So. there is no monopoly, there is no preference, and everything is done for the advantage of the port. Now, without going further, there is a question whicli has been treated more or less during this debate, the question whether the port of Montreal has ever been helped by the government and how that has been done. It lias been done in other places. I have in my hand figures procured for the harbour commissioners in Montreal in 1898, when we began the discussion of this question. The report of John M. Wilson, brigadier-general of the United States army, goes to show the following facts with regard to the ports in the United States. Boston harbour has been helped by the Federal government to the extent of $1,271,000 in round figures ; New York, $4,701,000 ; Philadelphia harbour, including Delaware river, $5,000,000 ; Baltimore harbour, $2,500,000. Now, in Canada, what have we been doing as regards the helping of ports out of public money ? We have a statement, which has been filed before this House, in reply to an interpellation by Mr. Lepine, who was a member of this House for the St. Mary's division of Montreal, on the 6th of February, 1893. This shows that the amount of $17.835,420 has been voted by the Dominion government since 1867 in improving harbours, building breakwaters, dredging, &c. According to the list I hold in my hand, it appears that not a cent has been siaent in the port of Montreal by this government or by aiiy government. The only amount that can be said to be charged to Montreal is the debt that was assumed by the government in 18S0 or 1887. of about $3,000,000. which has been spent by the harbour commissioners in dredging the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal. That amount had been levied on the trade and commerce done in the port of Montreal, and it was only fair and reasonable that the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal should be reimbursed for this amount, and that the debt should be assumed by the Dominion government. From that time up to the present, not a single cent has been paid by the Dominion government for improvements in the port of Montreal, and unless the government is disposed to take over the debt of the harbour commissioners that I have .-Just mentioned, and assume the management of the port; the commissioners will have to continue to levy dues upon commerce, and will have to devise some means of obtain-Mr. PREFONTAINE.
i ns' a revenue from the trade coming into Montreal so as to meet the interest on the debt that they7 are authorized to incur.
1 may mention to the House that other countries have expended large sums in improving their ports. There is nothing extraordinary in that. There is no reason why the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) and the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) should oppose any grants that may be made to the St. Lawrence route, in view of the amounts which other countries have spent in improving their harbours. England has not hesitated a moment in spending at different times $1.000.000, $80,000,000 and $60,000,000 to improve its port at London. Belgium has spent $30,000,000 at Antwerp, and during its last session of parliament has appropriated another $15,000,000 to complete the harbour improvements at Antwerp on the north side of L'Escout. Holland has also spent $72,000,000 at Rotterdam and Amsterdam. Manchester has just spent $68,000,000 in order to afford navigation to seagoing vessels in its harbour without breaking bulk. Denmark, a small country, follows the example and creates a free port at Copenhagen, with a depth of 30 feet of water, at the cost of more than $25,000,000. France has spent $30,000,000 at Havre, $25,000,000 at Marseilles, and $12,000,000 at Bordeaux. In view of all these facts, are we to be blamed for insisting that the St. Lawrence should be made into a condition to accommodate at least the trade of our Canadian North-west, and if possible, to secure the greatest part of the trade of the western states ? I think the question should be discussed from a broad national point of view, rather than as regarding Montreal proper. I admit that the government since 1898 has regarded this question as a national one, and I hope they will still continue so to regard it.

I think the members of this House will conclude that this question has resolved itself into one between Montreal and Quebec, rather than into a broad and national question, from which point of view it should be considered. No Canadian who has the interest of his country at heart fails to recognize that this transportation question is one of the greatest problems that we have to grapple with. The discussion of this question which has taken place in the last parliament as well as during the present session, shows that our people are alive to the situation. But there are other features of this transportation question which must not be lost sight of. The member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) has spoken of the great competitor we have to the south of us. and, as he says, it is time that our Canadian people should wake up to this fact and put forth every possible effort in order to meet them where they are endeavouring to take

away trade from us. I do not propose tonight, however, to discuss the relative advantages of Montreal or Quebec. That is a very debatable question, but the facts that have just been stated by the hon. member for Maisonueuve (Mr. Prefontaiue) show that it is of the utmost interest to all Canada. He says that in 188(5 this government assumed a debt of 83,000.000, which had been incurred for dredging the River St. Lawrence, but he has not told us how many million dollars this country has spent there since 1886. Our people are now considering whether this transportation should not be continued a little further down the River St. Lawrence without breaking bulk.
I support the contention of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) as to the need of a most thorough hydrographic survey of Canadian coastal waters. I "believe there is nothing in which we are weaker than in this very respect. It is well known that the British Admiralty have for years given great attention to this subject, so that every rock and shallow "on the coast of Great Britain is as well known as the landmarks are. Even in Canada we have derived some advantage from the work of the British Admiralty along our coasts, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has told us. In discussing this matter of a winter port, we have only heard four or live ports mentioned. I would like to give the House a little information. We have been told about Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there is a county called Charlotte in the province of New Brunswick, and I want to tell you further that there are two of the best harbours on the Atlantic seaboard in that country. There is the harbour of Letang which was surveyed by Admiral Owen in 1842, and which lie stated was the best harbour from Florida to Newfoundland, a harbour capable of accommodating the whole British fleet. It has an advantage over the harbour of Montreal and some others in the fact that it lias no silt, it has no large river emptying its deposit into the harbour.
What is the rise and fall of the tide in this harbour ?

Nearly 30 feet, but it has less fog than the city of Halifax and some points on Cape Breton. Now, this hydrographic survey that has been referred to cannot be undertaken too soon. I have no disposition to say anything against the Gulf of St. Lawrence. I think it is only a year or two ago that a steamer ran on an unmarked rock in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and if proper provision had been made for a hydrographic survey, that accident would have been impossible. But how this matter shall be taken up is another question. Without doubt it presents many difficulties. There is no maritime country in the world
that is better equipped than Canada to improve its national waterways. We have the most magnificent fisheries in the world and we have employed in them an army of some 80,000 men. These men are all of good physique, men of intelligence, men of brawn and muscle, men inured to hardships from their very laborious work and they would make excellent auxiliaries if utilized for the carrying on of the work of the hydrographic survey. We are all the time increasing this army; in fact, the army is increasing more rapidly than we can utilize it. If you will look at the statistics of the Fisheries Department you will find that within the last five or six years some 15,000 of these stalwarts have been added to the fishing- fleets. But, we are furnishing this same brawn, brain and muscle to the United States, for if you look at the records of the Gloucester fishing fleet, you will see that there is hardly a vessel lost on the banks but lias amongst its crew men from Shelburne, from Guysborough. from Lunenburg or some other Nova Scotia or New Brunswick county. So that, we are supplying for the American fleet brawn, brain and muscle.
Now, Sir, these men are not adapted to farming. It is almost impossible to take a man from these districts and put him at successful farming. But, we want to keep our Canadians at home and if we would keep them at home we must make some provision for utilizing them. I would suggest something that I hope will be adopted in the future if not at present. I believe that this government, acting by itself, or in connection with the British government, could take up this matter in such a form that we will keep many of our young men who are leaving us to-day within our own borders, men who are ready to defend the empire and do honour to Canada as our soldiers have done in South Africa. I believe that we should have, as soon as possible, such arrangements made with Great Britain as will result in the fitting out of at least three auxiliary cruisers for our coastal waters, one for British Columbia, one for the Gulf of St. Lawrence and one for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and that these auxiliary cruisers should take this surplus of men that we have in the fishing fleet and train them for the navy so that when Great Britain requires assistance she will be able to get a good strong quota from her Canadian colony. The men themselves would like it. I understand that at the time the volunteers were asked for South Africa numerous applications were made from the islands in my county but because these men could not ride a horse they could not go. They can ride a taflfrail, or a spar, or a yard, but, if proper conditions in regard to this navy arrangement which I have suggested existed, we could have hundreds of these young men trained for the British navy, young men who would be very glad

to give their services. I have to-day applications from four or five districts in my county from fishermen who wish to form rifle clubs in order to put themselves in a position to be able to take their part in defence of the empire. Instead of furnishing a good quota for the American navy as we are doing to-day. we would have at least three training ships filled with Canadian blue-jackets ready to defend the interests of the empire, and if these three training ships were used for the purpose of the hydrographic survey, just as British ships "have been used around the coasts, we would derive great advantage from it. I would go farther ; if Great Britain would not take hold of this project with us, I would have Canada prepare three auxiliary cruisers herself so that we would have a class of ships that could be utilized in defence of the empire if it were necessary at any time. We would not then be furnishing brawn or brain to the nation to the south of us, or be furnishing men to that country who might be a menace to our independence at some time in the future. I do not propose to take up any more time of the House, but I believe if these suggestions were carried out we would, in a very few years, have our coastal service in such a condition that the coastal navigation of Canada would be equal to that of the British Islands.

Mr. Speaker, I trust that at this late hour of the night I will not have the bad taste to occupy the time of the House for more than a very few minutes. We have heard addresses from hon. gentlemen from the east, from Montreal, from Quebec, from the Atlantic coast, and while I have been very anxious to learn all I could upon the transportation question, the discussion seems to have narrowed itself down to the questions, as the last speaker (Mr. Ganong) has said, as to the most desirable port, whether it should be Montreal, or whether it should be Quebec. Now, I venture to say that this is a vastly larger question than is involved in that consideration of it. It is a question that will occupy, and should occupy a very great deal of the time of the best expert talent in the Dominion of Canada. The question of transportation does not involve only a matter of the point of shipment, whether it should be Quebec ; whether it should be Montreal, or Portland, or Boston. The question Involved is : How shall we obtain for the producers of Canada of every kind the best possible results for their labour and investments. Can that result be attained by attempting merely for the sake of what may be called patriotic motives, the forcing of freight and passengers up-hill ? I contend that the nearest port, the cheapest port to reach is the best port for Canada. The advantage accruing to the average man in this country from all its productions is the profit which remains in the hands of Mr. GANONG.
the producers after all expenses have been paid, and if our freight expenses, not only our freight expenses down through Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence to the sea, but those greater expenses from the Rocky Mountains to the headwaters of Lake Superior, be added to the expenses of placing our goods on the market in England it is a matter that should occupy the attention, as I said before, of experts. A suggestion was made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that I most heartily endorse. It is that the government should seriously consider the appointment of an expert commission outside of this House which would sit year in and year out, take evidence and report to this House, season after season, the result of their experience and of their consultations. I contend that this* would have the effect of doing far more for this country than an expenditure of $750,000 a year upon a fast passenger service to take passengers to and from the continent. I contend that a passenger service, however desirable in itself, is not nearly as desirable to this country as a first-class freight service. A first-class freight service which would have cold storage added to its facilities would be an advantage. We have heard a great deal about cold storage and have seen very little of it. I come, as hon. gentlemen; know, from Toronto and we see very little of cold storage there, but I contend that there should be better cold storage facilities in various parts of this country for the preservation of fruits, vegetables and all kinds of perishable commodities. There is an industry in the province of Ontario and which I think extends into the province of Quebec and it is the industry <?f canning fruits and vegetables. I attended a meeting a short time ago at which it was announced that last year there were 10,000,000 tins of fruit canned in this country, and that in consequence of the difficulty of placing them on the English market they were unable to export them and all had to be consumed at home. If we were able to properly export these goods there would be 30,000,000 cans produced within a short time, because there are more apples and other fruit rotting in our orchards than would supply the demands of the people of England.
At present there is great pressure brought to bear upon the government to expend vast sums of money on canals. I would not -take it upon myself to say that our past expenditure on canals has been all lost, but I am prepared to maintain the assertion that, any large future expenditure on canals would be a very great mistake. Canals have had their day, and railroads in all directions are surpassing and supplementing them. People nowadays want to get a return for their money quiekly, and they can only accomplish that by using railways to consign their products to the markets in preference to the slower means of shipping

fby canal routes. Whether or not there should be government control or government ownership of railways, as contended for by the hon. member for York (Mr. Maclean), I believe that whenever a railway receives a bonus from the country, the freight rates on that railway should be controlled by the government or by a commission appointed by the government. 1 would strongly urge the government not to spend any more large sums of money upon new canal systems. The Georgian Bay canal is spoken of to cost sixty or seventy million dollars, and other expensive canals are advocated. We gave a charter the other day to a railway, allowing it "bonding privileges for $10,000 a mile, a railway that would only be used when one steamer can meet it at the Georgian Bay, and another steamer meet it on Lake Ontario. This vast railway that is to cost such an enormous sum can only be used for six months in the year. I would again suggest that this vast subject of transportation should be taken hold of by the government appointing a commission to investigate it in all its hearings. I think Canada has an honest and solid claim upon the mother country, founded on the fact that it is not the fault of Canada that we have no better ports than we have to-day. It is the fault of Great Britain, who gave away those great ports which did belong to us and should belong to us.
Hear, hear.

Canada is not to blame for that. I place some responsibility upon the shoulders of the right hon. the Prime Minister, that when he was in England representing this country, he neglected that grand opportunity of using this argument with the British government, and asking them for privileges in their markets as some compensation for having given away those splendid harbours which should property belong to us. I believe that would be a strong argument, an argument that would prevail, aud an argument which would add somewhat to the enthusiasm that seems to be growing in favour of preferential trade between the mother lanid and her colonies. This is a matter which might also be taken into consideration by the commission which has been suggested by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). There is involved in it great questions that might occupy the attention of the cabinet ministers and of the great minds of this country, who have expert knowledge of matters connected with transportation. Facilities for the proper export of our produce is one thing, but. as the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) suggested, we have to do something in the line of bringing freight back to this country. To accomplish that we must have population. and to get population we must demonstrate to the people of Europe that we have in Canada vast advantages over the country to the south of us. I do not believe that
even the members of this House who have not been to the Pacific coast can realize the wonderful resources of this country, its enormous extent, and its vast areas of arable land yet unfilled. If this matter is property handled, I believe that before many years there will he such a population in this country as will astonish us, and that even those of us who are growing old will live to be so astonished. Our concern is not only to find the nearest, cheapest and quickest way to the markets of Europe, but it is as well to demonstrate in these markets the richness and the productiveness of our country. A moment ago I spoke of the canned fruit trade, and to give an idea of the possibilities of that industry if we could find a market, I may state that from the province of Ontario alone we could supply all the canned fruits aud vegetables required for the English market. Coming from the interior of the country, as I do, I am not here to advocate the city of Montreal, or the city of Quebec, or the city of Halifax, as the national port. The great question for us to consider is not the merits of any one port, but the general interests of the whole Dominion. If it is desirable to double-track some of our railroads, I believe that the government should assist in that work rather than spend large sums of money upon canals. I believe that the government should take great care, however, to retain in their own hands, that power which I fear they have not now of regulating the freight rates on our railway system.
We have heard a good deal in this House about the insurance question, and about the difficulty of getting vessels to come to Montreal, in consequence of the high rate of insurance. That is a question which like the waters of the great St. Lawrence, will find its own level. Banking institutions are seeking investments in this country, and if there is a good route by way of Montreal or any other, money will be found to seek investment in insurance and in everything else connected with our trade, at a reasonable rate of interest on the investment. Sir, I want more evidence, and I think the country wants more evidence, as to what scheme should be devised for best promoting the trade of the country. I believe that before any expenditure is undertaken either in Montreal or Quebec, a commission should be appointed not only to inquire into this question, but generally to take into consideration the best interests of the whole Dominion, and I believe, Sir, that the recommendation of such a commission would have great weight with the public, and would tend to a proper conclusion as to wliat is best to be done in the best interests of Canada.

It may be thought somewhat strange that a person from an inland county should take any material interest in a subject such as this, but it seems to me that this is a ques-

tion of vital importance to every man, -woman and cliild living in tile Dominion of Canada.
We are told tliat history repeats itself. If that be so, is it not wise for us to look a little ahead and see what is going to take place in the future ? Let us look back a few years, for example, and note what has taken place in the United States. I remember very well when the Genesee valley in the state of New York was one of the great grain-growing centres of the United States. At that time Rochester was called the flour city, because it possessed so many wheatgrinding mills. That has all changed. The wheat growing has left the state of New York and gone to the western states. Comparatively none of that cereal is grown in the state of New York now. A still greater change has taken place. When the wheatgrowing area moved further west, people in New York state got their livelihood largely by raising cattle and manufacturing cheese and butter ; but, in a short space of time these industries also went west. Large manufacturing cities grew up in the state of New York, and the milk which formed the raw material of the cheese and butter factories was absorbed by the population of those cities ; milk trains went in every direction. To give an illustration, only a few years ago, the Standard Butter Company, of Owego, N.Y., manufactured .more butter than any other creamery in the world. To-day that creamery is practically closed, because it cannot get the raw material.
Now, what has taken place in the United States is more than likely to take place in Canada. To-day in the province of Ontario large quantities of cheese and butter are manufactured and exported ; but, we are also growing a large quantity of wheat. But the 'same thing which took place in the state of New York is going to take place in Ontario. Our wheat fields will be in the west ; our cheese and butter factories will be in the east; and in Ontario we shall have other kinds of factories, such as woollen factories and iron factories. We must prepare for these changes. We must provide proper facilities for transporting the manufactured goods which we are going to make in Ontario, in Quebec, and, perhaps, in the maritime provinces, and also for carrying grain, flour, cattle and dairy products from the western plains of this Dominion. In order to do that we must improve the St. Lawrence route, and make it as perfect as possible.
The first thing to be done is for the government to make arrangements to provide facilities for the navigation of the St. Lawrence from the sea to Quebec and Montreal, so as to avoid the enormous insurance rates which have to be paid at present. Then, in the eastern portion of the Dominion we have wonderful facilities for manufacturing. We have such splendid water powers that Mr. WRIGHT. .
we can manufacture more cheaply here than in other parts of the Dominion. The construction of the Georgian Bay canal, which, I believe, will be constructed, will afford us a large addition of water power. Take the town of Cornwall, which has such large factories, or the town of Yalleyfield, and COte St. Paul, just outside of the city of Montreal. These places could never have had an existence if canals had not been constructed in their neighbourhood, furnishing them with water powers which the factories have utilized. Although the hon. member for Norfolk said that we would have difficulties in our canals such as they have in the Erie canal, and that the vessels would have to go so slowly and be so small that they could never compete with the railroads, I must differ entirely with him in that respect. The Erie canal is narrow for its whole distance, whereas the Georgian Bay canal will have large stretches of river navigation with a great depth of water, and only in the vicinity of waterfalls will the vessels have to go slowly. When that canal is constructed, such large water powers will be developed, that our manufactures will receive another impetus, and in the eastern part of the Dominion we shall be able to manufacture goods for the -western part of the Dominion, where they will grow grain and raise cattle.
With reference to the difficulty of loading and unloading cattle at the port of Montreal. I believe the time is not far distant when we shall not export our live cattle ; but they will be slaughtered here, giving employment to our people, and the hides and offal will be kept in the country for the benefit of our tanners and other manufacturers. When that is done we can export our chilled beef to the old country ; and, although we have no cases in Canada of rinderpest or pleuro-pneumonia such as they have in other countries, it will make no difference whether the authorities in the old country think we have them here or not, because we shall be exporting the chilled beef, which will go cheaper and better, and there will be more employment in our own country.
I do not propose, at this late hour of the night, to detain the House any longer ; but I believe this is a subject in which every man in Canada, no matter where he resides, is interested. It makes no difference to me whether the shipping facilities are greater in the city of Quebec or in the city of Montreal. What we want is cheap and excellent transportation for all the goods we manufacture in Ontario and the eastern provinces, and the very best and cheapest transportation for the products of the prairie provinces and the far west. I believe the time is not far distant when the head of navigation will not stop at Montreal, but will be carried farther west, and, perhaps, reach Fort William. That will be when our canals shall be deepened so that they will

compete with tlie railroads, and make them give us lower freights.
We all know that things are changing every day. It is within our recollection when a car could only hold 20,000 pounds, whereas to-day cars are manufactured that hold 73,000 to 80,000 pounds and some that will hold even more than that for the carriage of coal. The time was when an engine would only draw about twenty of these cars holding 20,000 pounds each, hut now there are these immense moguls which will haul 43 cars holding 70,000 pounds each, and the consequence is the railway lines can handle our freight much cheaper. And if we have cars and vessels that are growing in size, we must have large canals, and improved waterways and bring our waterways further into the interior, so that vessels can come right into the very centre of our country, where its products are grown and carry them at the lowest possible rate. I believe that the time is coming when our navigation will be deepened, and larger vessels will come further into the interior, and when that day comes an era of prosperity will dawn on us far exceeding anything yet dreamed of.
Hon. WILLIAM ROSS (Victoria, ISf.S.) At this late hour, I do not intend to take up much time, and would not have risen only it does not seem to be known in this House that we have a province called Nova Scotia and a harbour called Halifax. I was amused at the description of the New Brunswick harbour, where the smallest rise of the tide is about 30 feet. Why, in the harbour of Halifax, the ordinary rise is from 3} to 4 ieet, and the spring tides do not rise more than 0 feet. Besides that harbour is open all the year round, and within an hour from the time a steamer turns her face to the entrance, she is out in the open sea with nothing in the world before her except the vast expanse of ocean until she reaches the other side. But coming to Quebec or Montreal, once she passes between Cape North and Cape Ray and trims along the Magdalen Islands, she has to move slowly and cautiously and pick out her way in order to preserve life and property. Nothing of that kind is required in entering the port of Halifax. It is all very well to speak of those fresh-water ports, but it seems to me that the speeches made in connection with those ports were to some extent also a little fresh. When you come to speak of a harbour that is closed in the month of November and not open again until the month of May, there is no comparison between it and the harbour of Halifax. And not only are the ports of Quebec and Montreal closed during the winter season, but when they are open they are expensive ports. The pilotage is expensive, and I know that there would be a larger trade between Nova Scotia and those ports, were it not for the pilotage and other expenses which deter 103
vessels from going there to exchange cargoes. If you want to bring trade to Montreal and Quebec, you must cheapen everything in connection with the shipping of goods, and in that respect the harbour of Halifax is 50 per cent cheaper than either Montreal or Quebec. The great draw-'back to Montreal is the amount of improvements required to make it a successful shipping port. Nothing of that kind is required in Halifax. The harbour is deep and requires no dredging, and there are no rocks or shoals or other impediments in it. You can almost put your hands on the decks of the steamers as they come up and down outside our wharfs. We have every facility, and when those other places are asleep in the winter time you will see steamers running in and out of Halifax just as they do in summer.
What does Halifax need then to build up its port ? Why does not trade go there now ?
The trade is there now. The number of steamers that go in and out of the port of Halifax every day of the Week shows that it is.
Why then does not the trade of Canada go to so magnificent a port ?
The reason is the length of the haul by railway, which of course deters freight from going to Halifax.
The hon. gentleman's proposal then is to get lower railway rates.

What we require is lower rates over the Intercolonial Railway and greater speed in the transit of freight. Of course we are not advancing in this country in respect of our transit facilities as fast as they are in other countries, so that there is a great deal for us yet to learn in that respect. But I did not rise except to let the House know the advantages of the harbour of Halifax, which are superior to anything on this side of the Atlantic under British possessions.

FOWLER (King's, N.B.) I had not intended to take any part in this debate, but I notice that the most important harbour in all Canada has not yet received any attention. I refer now to the harbour of St. John, N.B.
It is a mud hole.
The hon. member for Victoria says it is a mud hole.
Yes, they are dredging there all the time.

It is not hid behind a bank of fog, as Halifax is, for a good portion of the year. It was only a short time ago that a steamer was obliged to lie to for two or three days outside Halifax as she could not get in on account of the fogs.
